然而，访问梅拉图斯山脉的许多保护主义者，都致力于通过以社区为基础的保护来赋权梅拉图斯人。为什么这个基本上很好的想法，会造成一些与军事化和腐败的发展政策相同的有问题的动态？倡导者被推到与梅拉图斯社群领袖大致相同的位置：如果他们不用国家、国家精英和国际专家可识别的话语来描绘资源与社群，他们的倡导就完全无效。在这种背景下，倡导者以与其受众最深恐惧相反的方式来表现乡村社群：他们说，这些人被组织成服从的社群，有清晰的领导结构、合理的管理政策和明确划定的领土。剩下要做的，就是给予这些社群权利。20

原页 199, 200

As advocacy this is proper and important, even with its assumptions: a unified and stable community; clearly stated management plans; and traditional customary territory. I don’t think advocates are able to operate without winning images and frameworks. Yet perhaps there is some room here to maneuver—and room to learn.

原页 199, 200

作为倡导，这是恰当而重要的，即使带有这些假设：一个统一稳定的社群；明确陈述的管理计划；传统习惯领土。我不认为倡导者能在没有有吸引力的形象和框架的情况下运作。不过，这里也许还有一些回旋余地——也有学习余地。

原页 200

And so, I emphasize again the practices that link humans and nonhumans in creating the social-natural landscape. Practices show us how landscape biodiversity is materially appreciated; they lead us to questions about particular human-nonhuman relationships and away from barren debates about the wisdom or stupidity of primitive people. Instead of basing rights claims on equivalents to private property, we might train our vision on the overlapping socialities of familiar forests, as these empower and constrain individuals in using forest resources. For example, even planted Meratus trees of any stature have multiple claimants: the descendants, male and female, of the original planter. No claimant can expect to profit from the tree alone. Forest management is facilitated, not hampered, by such overlapping and diverse claims (for example, rights to share in the product; see Tsing 2003a). Overlapping claims are a form of “community” through which forests are maintained. Interspecies socialities are embedded in the forest landscape. Processes of forging human-nonhuman relationships within dynamic, changing forests are as important here as forest boundaries.

原页 200

因此，我再次强调在创造社会—自然地景中连接人与非人的实践。实践向我们展示地景生物多样性如何在具体的物质实践中受到重视；它们把我们引向关于特定人类—非人类关系的问题，远离关于原始人智慧或愚蠢的贫瘠辩论。与其把权利主张建立在等同于私有财产的基础上，我们也许可以把目光训练到熟悉森林重叠的社会性上，因为这些社会性赋权并约束个人使用森林资源。例如，即使是梅拉图斯人栽种的稍成规模的树木，也有多个认领者：原栽种者的男女后代。任何认领者都不能指望独享树木的收益。这种重叠而多样的认领（例如分享产品的权利；见 Tsing 2003a）促进而非阻碍森林管理。重叠的认领是一种“社群”形式，森林通过它得到维护。跨物种社会性嵌入森林地景之中。在动态变化的森林中锻造人类—非人类关系的过程，在这里与森林边界同样重要。

原页 200

Landscape and Memory

原页 200

地景与记忆

原页 200

The Meratus forest is full of named locations. If Meratus do not lose themselves too often in the forest, it is not because they have a spiritual gift of navigation, as some romantics have claimed, but rather because they orient themselves to known places. Ridges, peaks, and saddles have names, as do prominent rocks and even insignificant creeks and springs and the distinctive pools, falls, and confluences of rivers. Many big trees also have names, that is, not only names for the kind of tree but also individual, personal names. Hillsides are commonly referred to in relation to the name of a big tree. Through these markers, hikers learn their way in the forest and, later, craft their tales of places and events.21

原页 200

梅拉图斯森林里到处是命名地点。如果梅拉图斯人不太常在森林中迷路，并非因为如某些浪漫主义者所称，他们有导航的灵性天赋，而是因为他们以已知地点来定位自己。山脊、山峰和鞍部都有名字，突出的岩石、甚至不起眼的小溪和泉眼，以及河流独特的深潭、瀑布和汇流处也都有名字。许多大树也有名字，不只是树种名称，还有个体的专名。山坡通常借助一棵大树的名称来指称。通过这些标记，徒步者学会在森林中认路，并在后来编织关于地点和事件的故事。21

原页 200, 201

Forest regrowth also orients the hiker: It tells the story of past swiddens as well as forest management. Even without knowing the people who once lived there, Meratus hikers learn something of the social history of the forest through observing the forest regrowth. In their own familiar forests, this regrowth is a place of memory, whether of one’s own past or that of one’s kin and neighbors. Hiking through familiar secondary forest, we often spoke of the stories from the past that forest regrowth told. Even relaxing at home, Meratus are likely to tell stories of their own pasts in relation to the sites they made swiddens as well as the places they traveled. The landscape becomes a medium for telling stories of oneself and others. At one point, I collected “swidden biographies,” that is, narrations of the consecutive swidden sites of each household. Since old swidden sites are not exclusive property claims, I found myself surprised at how easily their sites—and sights—rolled off people’s tongues.22 They were easy to tell because the narration of personal history through landscape has been an ordinary genre for speaking about one’s past.

原页 200, 201

森林再生也为徒步者定向：它讲述过去刀耕火种田以及森林管理的故事。即使不认识曾在那里居住的人，梅拉图斯徒步者也能通过观察森林再生，了解森林社会历史的一些东西。在他们自己熟悉的森林中，这种再生是记忆之地，无论记忆的是自己的过去，还是亲属和邻居的过去。徒步穿过熟悉的次生林时，我们常常谈起森林再生所讲述的往昔故事。即使在家休息，梅拉图斯人也可能讲述自己过去的故事，既涉及他们开垦刀耕火种田的地点，也涉及他们旅行过的地方。地景成为讲述自己与他人故事的媒介。有一段时间，我收集“刀耕火种传记”，即每户家庭连续刀耕火种地点的叙述。既然旧刀耕火种地点并非排他性财产认领，我惊讶地发现，他们的地点——以及景象——如此轻易地脱口而出。22它们容易讲述，是因为通过地景叙述个人历史，一直是谈论自己过去的普通体裁。

原页 201

Habits of attentiveness, practices of naming, and genres of telling make the forest intelligible for its Meratus residents. The forest appears neither particularly frightening nor wild; it is not outside the bounds of history and civility. Once one considers the possibilities of this kind of forest intelligibility, it seems likely that people all over the world must have come to know forests as social, historical, biographical spaces. How is it that this has been so hard to recognize? What work has it taken to repress the social intelligibility of the forest? These questions bring us back to habits of thinking about nature as global and transcendent, and why these habits have traveled anywhere at all, even if they have not reordered the landscape of the Meratus Mountains.

原页 201

关注的习惯、命名的实践和讲述的体裁，使森林对梅拉图斯居民来说可理解。森林既不特别可怕，也不特别野性；它并未超出历史与文明的界限。一旦考虑这种森林可理解性的可能，全世界的人想必都曾把森林认识为社会性、历史性、传记性的空间。为何这一点如此难以被承认？压抑森林社会可理解性，需要付出什么样的工作？这些问题把我们带回把自然视为全球性和超越性的思维习惯，以及这些习惯为何能传播到任何地方，即使它们并未重新安排梅拉图斯山脉的地景。

原页 201

One might again recall how hard European states had to work to evict peasants from their forests.23 Only by seizing the forests for elites, thus making forests, coercively, off-limits for peasant uses, did European forests become empty and wild. In this state they could be what one literary critic calls “the shadow of civilization,” that is, nonsocial spaces that haunted European sociality (Harrison 1992). The histories and prehistories of nationalism inscribed in European forests that Simon Schama (1995) tells in delineating a distinctly European set of regimes of “landscape and memory” require forests that have already been claimed for the shadows of nationalist elite imaginations.

原页 201

人们可以再次回想，欧洲国家曾费多大力气，才把农民逐出他们的森林。23只有为精英夺取森林，从而强行禁止农民使用森林，欧洲森林才变得空无而野生。在这种状态下，它们才能成为一位文学批评家所谓的“文明的影子”，即萦绕欧洲社会性的非社会空间（Harrison 1992）。西蒙·沙玛（1995）在勾勒一套独特的欧洲“地景与记忆”体制时讲述的、铭刻在欧洲森林中的民族主义历史与史前史，以森林已被纳入民族主义精英想象中的阴影领域为前提。

原页 201

This notion of forests as empty, wild, and available for elite manipulation also formed part of the repertoire of colonial scientists in their quest to understand the environment at the peripheries of European empire (Grove 1995). Forests were a key component of the discovery of this environmental form of “nature,” which, these scientists learned, could be used for European profit but also destroyed beyond repair. They watched European settlers cut down forests; they worried about erosion, loss of species, and climate change. But their attention both to the settlers’ use of forests and to forest protection assumed forests that were outside of long-term social occupation. These could not be forests that formed social “homes” because then they would be available for neither profit nor protection. They learned to observe empty forests, spaces of a nonsocial nature.

原页 201

森林作为空无、野生且可供精英操纵的观念，也构成殖民科学家在试图理解欧洲帝国边缘环境时所用的一套观念的一部分（Grove 1995）。森林是发现这种环境形式“自然”的关键组成部分；这些科学家得知，这种自然可用于欧洲的利润，但也可能被毁得无法修复。他们看着欧洲定居者砍伐森林；他们担忧侵蚀、物种丧失和气候变化。但他们既关注定居者对森林的使用，也关注森林保护，其前提都是森林处在长期社会占用之外。这些森林不能是形成社会“家园”的森林，因为那样它们就既不能用于利润，也不能用于保护。他们学会观察空无的森林，即非社会自然的空间。

原页 202

Learning both with and against the natives whose territories they had come to occupy, colonial scientists concluded that this profitable-yet-fragile nature was transcendent, beyond the circumscribed knowledge of any given vernacular culture. Writing to each other from one imperial corner to another, they found that this universal nature was also global, that is, interconnected across the planet. The discourse on deforestation—as necessary to human enterprise yet a cause of systematic environmental deterioration—formed a centerpiece of this discussion of a “nature” that could travel across cultures and across empires.

原页 202

殖民科学家与他们前来占领其领土的原住民既合作又对抗地学习，得出结论：这种既有利润又脆弱的自然具有超越性，超出任何特定地方性文化有限的知识。他们从一个帝国角落写信给另一个帝国角落，发现这种普遍自然也是全球性的，即在整个星球上相互联系。关于森林砍伐的话语——它既是人类事业所必需，又造成系统的环境退化——成为这场关于一种能跨越文化、跨越帝国传播的“自然”讨论的核心。

原页 202

When this imperial discourse spread in the twentieth century to inform international development and conservation expertise, the central place of forests was not disturbed. Yet these “forests” are a very particular object, inherited from European state-making and empire-building. Forests are recognizable around the world only to the extent that they are empty and wild, the shadows of civilization. Where indigenous people are recognized within them, international discussion makes the people wild things too, assimilated to the wild emptiness of the forest. Their social lives come out to meet the international public only across a deep abyss; they flit through the forest like birds. In contrast, a more recognizable set of rural people is known in the forest, but as a destructive force: poor peasants. Represented as just ordinary folks, poor people are said to destroy the forest to make their meager living. Third World elites blame them to explain why the forests are disappearing. One sees here the resiliency of the concept of nonsocial forests. If forests are being destroyed, it is society; if they aren’t, it is nature: Everything can be explained by placing it somewhere in the dichotomy of social and natural.

原页 202

当这种帝国话语在20世纪传播开来，为国际发展与保护专业知识提供信息时，森林的中心地位并未受到扰乱。然而这些“森林”是一个非常特殊的对象，继承自欧洲的国家建构与帝国建设。森林只有在空无而野生、作为文明之影的程度上，才在世界各地被识别。当原住民在其中被承认时，国际讨论也把人变成野性之物，同化于森林的野生空无。他们的社会生活只有跨越一道深渊才出来与国际公众相见；他们像鸟一样掠过森林。相比之下，一类更容易辨识的乡村人群在森林中为人所知，却是作为破坏性力量：贫穷农民。穷人被表现为普通百姓，据说是为了维持微薄生计而毁坏森林。第三世界精英责备他们，以解释森林为何正在消失。在此可见非社会森林概念的韧性。如果森林正被摧毁，那是社会；如果没有，那是自然：只要把一切放进社会与自然的二分法，就都能解释。

原页 202

The Meratus Mountains have not escaped the gaze stimulated by this framework, but rather are repeatedly inscribed. The Social Welfare Department saw “social” people destroying “natural” forests and tried to resettle the people out of the forests. The loggers saw empty, natural forest and came in to log it. The plantation operators saw forest degraded by society and needing to be restored to nature—in a monocrop, profitable form. I could continue. But this is not everything that is going on. There are other forests here too: the social-natural forests of Meratus residents. To see these forests, a change in perspective is required. I mark this change of perspective in the idea of “gaps.” Gaps develop in the seams of universal projects; they are found where universals have not been successful in setting all the terms. While a transcendent, nonsocial, global “nature” has become a powerful thing worldwide, it is not the only kind of nature on the planet. Whenever we want to trace the limits of hegemony, we need to look for gaps. An ethnography of global connection is impossible without this tool.

原页 202

梅拉图斯山脉并未逃脱这一框架所激发的凝视，反而被反复铭写。社会福利部看到“社会性”的人在毁坏“天然”森林，试图把人迁出森林重新安置。伐木者看到空无的天然森林，进来采伐。种植园经营者看到因社会活动而退化的森林，需要恢复为自然——以单一作物、有利可图的形式。我可以继续列举。但这不是事情的全部。这里还有别的森林：梅拉图斯居民的社会—自然森林。要看见这些森林，需要改变视角。我用“空白”这一观念标记这种视角变化。空白在普遍工程的接缝中发展；它们出现在普遍物未能成功设定所有条件的地方。虽然一种超越的、非社会的、全球的“自然”已成为世界上强大的事物，但它不是地球上唯一的自然。每当我们想追踪霸权的局限，就需要寻找空白。没有这一工具，全球联结的民族志不可能完成。

第三部　自由

停止！

原书分部扉页展示反对开发梅拉图斯山脉的宣传海报，标题为“STOP! EKSPLOITASI PEGUNUNGAN MERATUS”，署名ALIANSI MERATUS及KHAM；本版未复制图像。

原页 205

“A hair in the flour”

原页 205

“面粉里的一根头发”

原页 205

[Voice and freedom]

原页 205

［声音与自由］

原页 205

How does one speak out against injustice and the destruction of life on earth? Words and concepts betray us. The concept of freedom is much abused, and yet the idea of freedom is still as important a tool as any for the disenfranchised. Movements split and change. What seems at first empowerment can come to seem an oppressive discipline or an empty rhetoric. To pick among the causes presented to us—as well as those hidden from our view—is a constant work of passion and judgment. It changes who we are. We imagine that we find our “voice” for that moment when a way we have learned to speak seems to fit a critical purpose. We tap into a legacy of speaking to articulate our situation within a general complaint.

原页 205

人如何发声反对不义与对地球生命的毁灭？词语和概念背叛我们。自由的概念遭到严重滥用，然而自由的观念对被剥夺权利的人来说，仍是重要性不亚于任何其他工具的工具。运动分裂并改变。起初看似赋权的东西，后来可能显得像压迫性的纪律或空洞的修辞。在呈现给我们的各种事业——以及那些藏在我们视野之外的事业——中作出选择，是激情与判断的持续工作。它改变我们是谁。我们想象，当某种我们学会的说话方式似乎适合某个批判目的时，我们在那一刻找到了自己的“声音”。我们接入一份言说的遗产，把自己的处境表达为一种更普遍的抗议的一部分。

原页 205

The New Order regime in Indonesia came to power in 1966 by silencing one kind of voice and promoting another. The nationalist populism that had been increasingly identified with the Indonesian Communist Party was shattered in gunfire and buried in prison camps. The new state encouraged instead the voice of modernization and development. Citizens were asked to remake themselves in that modern discipline that promised future prosperity for both individuals and communities. Indeed, the greatest success of the New Order state in the countryside was the fact that so many rural people came to speak in this development voice. Their worst complaints could be solved, it seemed, by more development—that is, the expansion of the state. Most social analysts quickly naturalized this voice as the proper desire of the poor for self-improvement.

原页 205

印尼的新秩序政权于1966年上台，其方式是让一种声音沉默，并推广另一种声音。此前日益与印尼共产党联系在一起的民族主义民粹主义，在枪火中被粉碎，被埋葬在拘禁营中。新国家转而鼓励现代化与发展的声音。公民被要求以那种现代纪律重塑自己，它承诺个人与社群都将获得未来的繁荣。确实，新秩序国家在乡村的最大成功，是那么多乡下人开始用这种发展声音说话。他们最严重的抱怨似乎可以通过更多发展——也就是国家的扩张——来解决。大多数社会分析者很快把这种声音自然化为穷人要求自我改善的正当愿望。

原页 205, 206

Yet even at the height of New Order rule, other voices could be heard. The echoes of Indonesia’s anti-colonial struggle continued to reverberate in criticisms of corruption and calls for social justice. Critics of the state aligned themselves with varied transnational coalitions, ranging from Islam to environmentalism. Rhetorics of morality, on the one hand, and rights, on the other, came to fill the silences left by an earlier populism. Those who gravitated toward cosmopolitan, secular freedoms endorsed causes of human rights, the rule of law, and freedom of the press. Transnational political liberalism thus came to play a role in stimulating Indonesian critical voices.

原页 205, 206

然而即使在新秩序统治的鼎盛时期，也能听到其他声音。印尼反殖民斗争的余响继续在对腐败的批评和伸张社会正义的呼声中回荡。国家的批评者与各种跨国联盟结盟，从伊斯兰教到环保主义。一方面是关于道德的修辞，另一方面是关于权利的修辞，填补了早先民粹主义留下的沉默。那些被世界主义、世俗自由吸引的人，支持人权、法治和新闻自由的事业。跨国政治自由主义因而在激发印尼批判声音中发挥了作用。

原页 206

Environmental protection and social justice coalesced in this current. In the environmental movement of the 1980s and 1990s, rights discourse—human rights, customary property rights, indigenous cultural rights—addressed the intertwined problems of landscape destruction and authoritarian rule. Yet the relevance of rights to the problems at hand was not self-evident; it had to be established step by step, and often in a confused dance in which even partners stepped on each other’s feet. Terms were translated back and forth from foreign languages and across multiple vernacular uses. Local viewpoints proliferated, and angry debates flourished. As in any movement, it was often difficult to differentiate allies from enemies. Social criticism and political mobilization could only advance through friction.

原页 206

环境保护与社会正义在这股潮流中汇合。在20世纪80和90年代的环保运动中，权利话语——人权、习惯财产权、原住民文化权利——回应了地景破坏与威权统治相互交织的问题。然而，权利与眼前问题的相关性并非不言自明；它必须一步一步地建立起来，而且往往是在一场混乱的舞蹈中，甚至舞伴也会踩到彼此的脚。术语在外语与本地语言之间来回翻译，并在多种地方性用法中转换。地方观点激增，激烈的辩论蓬勃展开。如同任何运动，往往很难区分盟友与敌人。社会批评和政治动员只能通过摩擦推进。

原页 206

One place to begin is with some very parochial stories. My own attempts to find a voice frame those of my companions in the Meratus Mountains.

原页 206

一个起点是一些非常地方性的故事。我自己寻找声音的尝试，为我在梅拉图斯山脉的同伴们的尝试提供了框架。

···
原页 206

1986. After many years of political quietude in the countryside, people are talking. In the Meratus Mountains, the talk is of timber companies, which are destroying Meratus forests. I have been spending the summer in a mountainous area not yet in the range of the loggers, but people know that the loggers are moving up the slopes on both sides. When I hike down to the Meratus resettlement village of Niwan, the renowned shaman Awat Kilay, a mentor of mine, pulls me aside. “The logging companies are ruining our land,” he tells me. “When you go to Jakarta, you must tell Ibu Tien to stop.” Ibu Tien is the wife of then-president Suharto, and popularly imagined as the sponsor of much resource exploitation. I protest that I don’t have the status to make an appointment with Ibu Tien. He tries to talk me through it, conjuring an image of a pleasant lunch with the First Lady sipping tea. The task is urgent! I am embarrassed; I don’t know how to explain my weakness and my lack of courage. I tell him that all I know how to do is write. He becomes thoughtful, taking in my explanation. He tells me to write with a critical attitude. “Be a hair in the flour,” he explains. He is speaking of the rice flour used to prepare ritual cakes for the appeasement of authority. Communities offer ceremonial cakes to the spirits to keep them from taxing and troubling their human subjects; so, too, such appeasement is understood as the stuff of obedience to the state. A hair in the flour is a disturbance of everyday subservience and routine. A hair in the flour ruins the legitimacy of power. It is a benediction for my work and an inspiration for what I must continue to learn. I have repeated it to myself throughout the research for this book and its writing.

原页 206

1986年。在乡村多年的政治沉寂之后，人们开始议论。在梅拉图斯山脉，议论的是正在毁坏梅拉图斯森林的木材公司。我整个夏天都在一个尚未进入伐木者范围的山区度过，但人们知道伐木者正从两侧山坡向上推进。当我徒步下到梅拉图斯人的重新安置村尼万时，著名萨满阿瓦特·基莱——我的一位导师——把我拉到一边。“伐木公司正在毁掉我们的土地，”他告诉我。“你去雅加达时，必须告诉蒂恩夫人停下来。”蒂恩夫人是时任总统苏哈托的妻子，在民间想象中是许多资源开发的赞助者。我辩解说，我没有地位去预约会见蒂恩夫人。他试图说服我，想象第一夫人品着茶、共进愉快午餐的画面。任务紧迫！我很尴尬；我不知道如何解释我的软弱和缺乏勇气。我告诉他，我只会写作。他若有所思，接受了我的解释。他叫我带着批判态度去写。“做面粉里的一根头发，”他解释说。他说的是用来制作安抚权威的仪式糕饼的米粉。社群向精灵献上仪式糕饼，以免它们向人类臣民征税和找麻烦；同样，这种安抚也被理解为服从国家的东西。面粉里的一根头发是对日常服从与常规的扰乱。面粉里的一根头发毁掉权力的合法性。这是对我工作的祝福，也是对我必须继续学习之物的启发。在本书的研究和写作过程中，我一直对自己重复这句话。

原页 207

To write as a hair in the flour is to look for weaknesses, confusions, and gaps in business as usual. Without such friction, why would we bother to try to change anything? As a hair in the flour I tell of utopian social movements even where they are not victorious. These movements keep alive our sense that the forms of hierarchy and coercion we take most for granted can yet be dislodged. If I tell more about mobilizations for environmental protection and social justice than I do of suffocating development initiatives, it is to offer the former the chance to rattle the hegemony of the latter.

原页 207

作为面粉里的一根头发去写作，就是寻找一切照常运转中的弱点、混乱和空白。没有这样的摩擦，我们为什么要费心去改变什么？作为面粉里的一根头发，我讲述乌托邦社会运动，即使它们并未获胜。这些运动让我们保持一种感觉：我们最视为理所当然的等级与强制形式仍然可以被撼动。如果我更多讲述环境保护与社会正义的动员，而较少讲述令人窒息的发展举措，那是为了给前者一个机会，去撼动后者的霸权。

原页 207

But let me return to 1986. One evening, when family and friends have gathered, Awat Kilay gives a rousing speech. “The timber companies are colonizers!” he declares. “We fought the colonizers in the revolution, and we can fight them again!” I am struck that he uses the rhetoric of Indonesia’s struggle for independence. The timber company in this area is Indonesian, but that does not blunt its alien status. The trope of liberation seems quite right. It is a magnificent speech. But I doubt that it moves the young men whom he is trying most to impress. The young men are divided among themselves and cautious in assessing the words of Awat Kilay, who has spent many years living with the stigma of arrest and harassment for having attended a Communist-inspired land reform workshop in the 1960s. Awat Kilay’s son, Ma Igul, is handsome and ambitious, but better known for entrepreneurial than political endeavor. His family jokes that he has twice converted to Islam, and twice been circumcised, to improve his connections with Muslim traders. My adopted brother Ma Salam, a nephew of Awat Kilay, aspires to political leadership in his own mountain village of Rajang but holds a grudge against Awat Kilay for an imagined slight in his childhood. The awkward relation between these three alone is enough to divide communal sentiment—and to stop me from romanticizing Meratus Dayaks as a united cultural force. Instead, I must pick through the fragments and consider my possibilities of dialogue with each.

原页 207

但让我回到1986年。一天晚上，家人朋友聚在一起，阿瓦特·基莱发表了一场振奋人心的演讲。“木材公司是殖民者！”他宣称。“我们在革命中与殖民者战斗过，我们可以再次与他们战斗！”我注意到他使用了印尼争取独立的修辞。这个地区的木材公司是印尼公司，但这并未削弱其外来者地位。解放的比喻似乎相当恰当。这是一场宏大的演讲。但我怀疑它是否打动了他最想打动的那些年轻人。年轻人内部有分歧，而且在评价阿瓦特·基莱的话时很谨慎；他因20世纪60年代参加过一个共产党启发的土地改革工作坊，多年来一直生活在被捕和骚扰的污名中。阿瓦特·基莱的儿子马·伊古尔英俊而有野心，但更为人知的是创业而非政治事业。他的家人开玩笑说，他两次皈依伊斯兰教、两次行割礼，以改善与穆斯林商人的关系。我的结义兄弟马·萨拉姆是阿瓦特·基莱的侄辈，渴望在自己山中的拉让村获得政治领导权，却因童年时想象中的一次怠慢而对阿瓦特·基莱怀恨在心。仅这三人之间别扭的关系，就足以分裂社群情感——也足以阻止我把梅拉图斯达雅克人浪漫化为一股统一的文化力量。相反，我必须梳理碎片，并考虑我与每个人对话的可能性。

原页 207, 208

Luckily, Meratus mobilization against logging does not depend on this little gathering. It is centered not in Niwan or Rajang, where the loggers have not yet encroached, but in the adjacent village of Manggur. Through a somewhat inadvertent coalescence of activists, nature lovers, and village elders (in this case, a tightly united sibling set), a small victory is achieved, and the logging company is asked to leave village forests in this area alone. (I tell the story in chapter 7.) The logging company is so angry at being asked to leave that they destroy the area around their base camp, dumping gasoline and strewing machinery around the forest. For the next fifteen years, logging companies attack other areas of the Meratus Mountains, but they leave this sector alone. (Niwan, Rajang, and Manggur are on the west side of the Meratus Mountains. The frontier area I describe in chapter 1 is on the east side, where logging proceeds without pause.) Only in the late 1990s does activism from this sector once again take on an important role in giving voice to Meratus aspirations. The small victories and betrayals of this time—in which the earlier history of factions, transcriptions, and voicings of freedom bear fruit—make this a story worth telling to introduce the frictions of liberal politics.

原页 207, 208

幸运的是，梅拉图斯人反对伐木的动员并不依赖这次小聚会。它的中心不在伐木者尚未侵入的尼万或拉让，而在邻近的芒古尔村。通过活动家、自然爱好者和村中长者（这里是彼此紧密团结的一组兄弟姐妹）某种不经意间的汇聚，取得了一次小胜利，伐木公司被要求不要动这一地区的村有森林。（我在第七章讲述这个故事。）伐木公司对被要求离开如此愤怒，以至于毁坏了他们大本营周围地区，把汽油倒进森林，并将机械散置各处。此后十五年，伐木公司攻击梅拉图斯山脉的其他地区，却未再侵扰这一片地区。（尼万、拉让和芒古尔位于梅拉图斯山脉西侧。我在第一章描述的边疆地区位于东侧，那里伐木不间断地进行。）只有在20世纪90年代末，来自这一片区的活动主义才再次在赋予梅拉图斯人愿望以声音方面发挥重要作用。此时的小胜利与背叛——派系、转录和自由发声的更早历史在其中结出果实——使这个故事值得讲述，用以引入自由派政治的摩擦。

···
原页 208

In the 1990s, activism grew in Manggur, Rajang, and Niwan. Village leaders worked back and forth between different kinds of regional sponsors, mixing the rhetoric of development, on the one hand, and conservation, on the other. Community strength might be gathered from development grants, ecotourism, political patronage, property registration, or environmental advocacy: The most ambitious leaders aimed to draw them all to their villages. After the New Order fell in 1998, the national political situation grew lively and confused. With their political sponsors in trouble, resource exploitation companies experienced a time of insecurity, and community options for protest widened. An archipelago-wide alliance of indigenous people gathered together in Jakarta in 1999 to demand redress for the state’s nonrecognition of their rights. Manggur elders were there representing Meratus Dayaks. It was a thrilling moment for the development of new political ambitions and dreams. “If the State does not acknowledge us, we will not acknowledge the State,” the delegates wrote in their report (AMAN 1999: 9). They went on to refuse state claims to their lands and resources, to reject the state’s labels for them, to criticize the use of the armed forces in domestic affairs, to note the importance of women’s equality, and to demand full participation in the political process.

原页 208

20世纪90年代，活动主义在芒古尔、拉让和尼万发展起来。村中领袖在不同类型的地区支持者之间来回运作，把发展修辞与保护修辞结合起来。社群力量可能从发展拨款、生态旅游、政治庇护、财产登记或环境倡导中汇聚起来：最有野心的领袖想把它们全都带到自己的村庄。1998年新秩序倒台后，国家政治局势变得活跃而混乱。随着政治赞助者陷入困境，资源开发公司经历了一段不安全时期，社群抗议的选择也扩大了。1999年，一个全群岛原住民联盟在雅加达集会，要求纠正国家对其权利的不承认。芒古尔的长者们代表梅拉图斯达雅克人出席了会议。这是发展新政治抱负与梦想的激动时刻。“如果国家不承认我们，我们也不承认国家，”代表们在报告中写道（AMAN 1999: 9）。他们进而拒绝国家对其土地和资源的主张，拒绝国家强加给他们的标签，批评在国内事务中使用武装部队，指出妇女平等的重要性，并要求充分参与政治过程。

原页 208, 209

In 1999, too, a new logging threat emerged in the central Meratus Mountains. In November, the regional government had announced an exchange of the sort misleadingly made famous as a “win-win” deal by the U.S. Clinton administration. In exchange for the conservation of a piece of logged-out forest near the east coast, the government would offer the heavily forested central Meratus Mountains to the Korea Development Company, known as Kodeco. The government planned a special economic zone on the east coast to complement Kodeco’s already thriving cement and plywood factories there. Planners hoped to use a small piece of Kodeco’s used-up logging concession in the area as a water catchment area for the special economic zone. But before environmental studies could be done on the feasibility of this idea, and while the special economic zone was still a gleam in a planner’s eye, Kodeco was already surveying the Meratus forests they proposed as their exchange (Chamin, Maha Adi, and Hatta 1999).

Activists at multiple levels organized against the plan. Thirty-three regionally based NGOs formed the Meratus Advocacy Alliance (Aliansi Advokasi Meratus) to advocate for the Meratus and their forests. They pointed out that the logging plan required the government to change the classification of a forest that had long been considered a watershed protection area. They reminded the public of great floods that followed previous episodes of logging. They researched biodiversity and surveyed the opinions of Meratus residents of the forest. They contacted national and international news media, asking them to bring the eyes of the world to their campaign (Aliansi Advokasi Meratus 2000).

原页 208, 209

也是在1999年，中梅拉图斯山脉出现了新的伐木威胁。11月，地区政府宣布了一项交换安排；这类安排被美国克林顿政府冠以误导性的“双赢”之名而广为人知。为换取东海岸附近一片采伐殆尽森林的保护，政府将把森林茂密的中梅拉图斯山脉提供给韩国开发公司，即 Kodeco。政府计划在东海岸建立一个经济特区，以补充 Kodeco 在那里已经兴旺的水泥和胶合板工厂。规划者希望把 Kodeco 在该地区已采伐殆尽的特许采伐区中的一小块地用作经济特区的集水区。但在对该设想可行性进行环境研究之前，在经济特区还只是规划者心中的初步构想时，Kodeco 就已经在勘测他们提议作为交换的梅拉图斯森林（Chamin, Maha Adi, and Hatta 1999）。

多个层面的活动家组织起来反对该计划。33个地区性非政府组织组成梅拉图斯倡导联盟（Aliansi Advokasi Meratus），为梅拉图斯人及其森林倡导。他们指出，伐木计划要求政府改变一片长期被视为水源保护区的森林的分类。他们提醒公众注意以往伐木之后发生的特大洪水。他们研究生物多样性，并调查森林中梅拉图斯居民的意见。他们联系国内外新闻媒体，请他们把世界的目光带向这场运动（Aliansi Advokasi Meratus 2000）。

原页 209

Meratus village leaders also became active in the campaign. Meetings were convened, bringing participants from many villages into common discussions of the problem. But as the campaign gained steam, Kodeco became active in its own Meratus patronage.1 Kodeco representatives identified key Meratus leaders, wowed them on helicopter tours of company operations, and offered them and their communities substantial “community development” funds in exchange for their support for Kodeco’s logging plans. This was money in hand, a real good as opposed to the unlikely success of environmentalist dreams. A number of leaders changed sides, offering their support for Kodeco’s plan for “development.”

原页 209

梅拉图斯村庄的领袖们也积极投入这场运动。会议召开，把许多村庄的参与者带入对问题的共同讨论。但随着运动势头增强，Kodeco 开始积极在梅拉图斯施行自己的庇护。1Kodeco 代表确定了关键的梅拉图斯领袖，用直升机参观公司作业让他们惊叹，并向他们及其社群提供大笔“社区发展”资金，以换取他们对 Kodeco 伐木计划的支持。这是实实在在到手的钱，与环保梦想渺茫的成功形成对比。一些领袖改变了立场，支持 Kodeco 的“发展”计划。

原页 209

By March 2000, the political scene was polarized. On March 13, forty anti-logging Meratus leaders gathered at the provincial capital. An NGO ally made the inflammatory statement that was used as a newspaper headline in the Banjarmasin Post (March 14, 2000): “We are ready to burn down Kodeco.” Meanwhile, a Meratus spokesperson offered a more sober explanation of the protest: “We declare that we reject the plan to change the classification of the forest and its nature reserves for Kodeco Timber Company” (ibid.). This was not to be the last word. On March 14, almost one hundred Meratus Dayaks appeared, and this time they were demonstrating for Kodeco. “We are ready to accept any investor who profits from the Meratus Mountains, because we also want to be prosperous,” said a spokesman (Banjarmasin Post, March 15, 2000).

原页 209

到2000年3月，政治场面极化。3月13日，40位反对伐木的梅拉图斯领袖在省会聚集。一位非政府组织盟友发表了煽动性言论，被《班贾尔马辛邮报》用作新闻标题（2000年3月14日）：“我们准备烧掉 Kodeco。”与此同时，一位梅拉图斯发言人对抗议作了更冷静的解释：“我们宣布，我们拒绝为 Kodeco 木材公司改变森林及其自然保护区分类的计划”（同上）。这还不是最后的话。3月14日，将近100名梅拉图斯达雅克人出现，这一次他们是来为 Kodeco 示威的。“我们准备接受任何从梅拉图斯山脉获利的投资者，因为我们也想繁荣，”一位发言人说（《班贾尔马辛邮报》，2000年3月15日）。

原页 209, 210

By this time, my old friend Awat Kilay had succumbed to tuberculosis, and the next generation had grown into roles as village leaders. Naturally, Ma Igul and Ma Salam, who never had been friends, were on opposite sides of the controversy. Ma Igul stood for the right to development. He spoke for the prosperity to be ushered in by the timber company, for the benefit of all entrepreneurs. He himself was ready to gather up the forest products from soon-to-be-logged areas to bring in that otherwise wasted wealth. In contrast, Ma Salam was a leader of the opposition, speaking for the rights of villages to manage their own resources. He led mapping exercises to define village territories and spoke to regional officials about the importance of village-based conservation and development. He worked with the Meratus Advocacy Alliance, showing them how to make their work locally relevant. But local factions had taken over the debate.

原页 209, 210

到这时，我的老朋友阿瓦特·基莱已因肺结核去世，下一代已担起村中领袖的角色。自然，从未做过朋友的马·伊古尔和马·萨拉姆在这场争议中站在对立面。马·伊古尔代表发展的权利。他为木材公司即将带来的繁荣发声，说这将惠及所有企业家。他本人也准备把即将被采伐地区的林产品收集起来，把那些本来会被浪费的财富换成钱。相比之下，马·萨拉姆是反对派领袖，为村庄管理自己资源的权利发声。他领导测绘工作以界定村庄领土，并向地区官员讲述以村庄为基础的保护与发展的重要性。他与梅拉图斯倡导联盟合作，教他们如何让自己的工作在地方上具有相关性。但地方派系已经接管了辩论。

原页 210

Regional factions were also at play. In 2000, resource licensing was decentralized, and centralized control was replaced with negotiations among district, regency, and provincial officials and the varied blocs that aimed to influence them. Anti-Kodeco Meratus were allied with nongovernment organizations, the west-side tourist industry (which saw the death of regional tourism with the destruction of the forests), and a number of regency-level government representatives from the west side. The pro-Kodeco faction included the newly elected governor and the east-side regency officials who were already deeply involved with Kodeco’s extensive operations. The governor was able to move the decision to the east-side regency, thus putting Kodeco’s bloc in charge. Debate, however, continued. “Environmental minister rejects Meratus switch but provincial government persists in carrying it out,” read one headline in March 2003 (Radar Banjar, March 18, 2003).

原页 210

地区派系也在起作用。2000年，资源许可权下放，集中控制被区、县和省级官员以及试图影响他们的各种集团之间的谈判取代。反 Kodeco 的梅拉图斯人与非政府组织、西侧旅游业（它看到森林被毁后区域旅游的死亡）以及一些西侧的县级政府代表结盟。亲 Kodeco 派包括新当选的省长，以及已经深度卷入 Kodeco 广泛业务的东侧县官员。省长把决定权转到东侧县，从而让 Kodeco 的集团掌权。然而辩论仍在继续。“环境部长拒绝梅拉图斯交换，但省政府坚持实施，”2003年3月的一条标题写道（Radar Banjar，2003年3月18日）。

原页 210, 211

Conventions of news reporting would suggest I stop the story there, with the delineation of factions. Yet this would ignore everything else that has happened in the province over the last twenty-five years. During that time, Kodeco has logged most of the east side of the Meratus Mountains, creating the frontier described in chapter 1. The ecological results have been dramatic, ranging from total loss of tree cover, to its replacement with monocrop plantations, to the skimpy residual forests that were so badly burned in the great fires of 1997. One can say unequivocally that the ecological function of the forest has been badly compromised, biodiversity drastically reduced, and erosion on slopes and river silting and flooding have become major problems. (To add insult to injury, Kodeco has designated some clearcut areas “community forests.”) Meanwhile, this destruction has not brought prosperity to the region and its inhabitants. Profits have been shipped out of the region. The luxury of Kodeco’s compound has not been reproduced in villages. Meratus residents have been politically and economically marginalized by the flood of migrants who have followed the frontier economy. Forest-based livelihoods are no longer possible. Where compensation has been offered for forest land and resources, it in no way matches what would be required to make a living. There are now some wrist watches, televisions, and motorcycles, but these are a poor substitute for agro-forestry livelihoods. With them have come hunger, poverty, and depression. To imagine that Kodeco would take more social or environmental responsibility in its logging of the remaining healthy forest—without even being pressed—is wishful thinking.

原页 210, 211

新闻报导惯例会建议我在划分派系后就此打住。然而这会忽略过去25年该省发生的一切。在此期间，Kodeco 采伐了梅拉图斯山脉东侧的大部分地区，制造了第一章描述的边疆。生态后果十分戏剧性，从树木覆盖完全丧失，到被单一作物种植园取代，再到1997年大火中严重烧毁的稀疏残存森林。可以毫不含糊地说，森林的生态功能遭到严重损害，生物多样性急剧减少，山坡侵蚀、河流淤积和洪水已成为主要问题。（雪上加霜的是，Kodeco 把一些皆伐区指定为“社区森林”。）与此同时，这种破坏并未给该地区及其居民带来繁荣。利润被运出该地区。Kodeco 大院的奢华没有在村庄中重现。梅拉图斯居民因追随边疆经济的移民潮而在政治上和经济上被边缘化。以森林为基础的生计不再可能。即使为林地和资源提供补偿，也远不足以维持生计。现在有一些手表、电视和摩托车，但它们是农林复合生计的糟糕替代品。与它们同来的是饥饿、贫困和抑郁。想象 Kodeco 在采伐剩余健康森林时会承担更多社会或环境责任——甚至无需别人施压——是一厢情愿。

原页 211

It is with this background information that one can see that the two sides of the struggle have rather different stakes. The pro-Kodeco faction hopes to get some trace of the wealth for themselves before it slips entirely out of the province. The anti-Kodeco faction wants to change the terms of the discussion. Their protests challenge the status quo of corporate privilege, rather than trying to make a small place inside its net. The implications of each are politically different—for the forests, for Meratus communities, and for the wider public in and beyond South Kalimantan. It is a great frustration to me that nothing I can think of to write seems likely in itself to tip the balance.

原页 211

正是在这种背景下，人们才能看出斗争双方的利害关系相当不同。亲 Kodeco 派希望趁财富完全滑出本省之前为自己分得一点财富。反 Kodeco 派想改变讨论的条件。他们的抗议挑战公司特权的现状，而不是试图在其网中谋得一个小位置。两者各自的影响在政治上是不同的——对森林、对梅拉图斯社群，以及对南加里曼丹内外更广泛的公众。令我非常沮丧的是，我能想到要写的任何东西本身似乎都不太可能改变平衡。

原页 211

Still, to write as a hair in the flour means to give the mobilization against forest destruction its due, not just to praise it, but to show how it offers a practical model to oppose global business as usual. How do we convince people that life on earth is worth saving? This is a political question as well as an environmental one. It requires a politics of working across difference in which the goal is not to make difference disappear but to make it part of the political program. Furthermore, the task requires the same breadth of global connection as does frontier resource extraction.

原页 211

尽管如此，作为面粉里的一根头发去写作，意味着给予反对森林破坏的动员应有的重视，不只是赞美它，还要展示它如何提供一种实践范式，去反对全球既有秩序照常运转。我们如何说服人们，地球上的生命值得拯救？这是一个政治问题，也是一个环境问题。它需要一种跨越差异运作的政治，其目标不是让差异消失，而是使它成为政治纲领的一部分。此外，这项任务需要与边疆资源开采同样广度的全球联结。

原页 211

Thus, ironically, it seems politically as well as intellectually useful to offer a symmetrical analysis of friction in both the resource extraction industry and its opposition. To show contingencies, gaps, and slippages interrupts claims of the easy unity of the market as it also illustrates the creative possibilities of social mobilization. Each requires attention to the awkwardness of translation and the need to build heterogeneous audiences.

原页 211

因此，讽刺的是，对资源开采业及其反对者双方的摩擦作对称分析，在政治上和智识上似乎都有用。展示偶然性、空白和滑移，打断了市场轻易统一的宣称，也说明了社会动员的创造性可能。两者都需要关注翻译的别扭，以及建构异质受众的需要。

原页 211, 212

Politics on both sides of the Kodeco debate involved rounding up local allies by deploying a full array of transnational resources. Kodeco was only offered the central Meratus Mountains as a concession because when informed of the plan to use a piece of its land as a water catchment area, it threatened to sue at the World Court (Chamin et al. 1999). Those who wanted to preserve the forest also spoke of the international context, for example, in attracting tourists, as one spokesperson argued, “from Holland, Australia, Canada, and the United States” (Dinamika Berita 1999). Yet the relation between transnationalism and regional mobilization differed on each side. The pro-Kodeco faction needed to cover up their transnationalism to make participants imagine a local populism. Their transnationalism is a reminder of the alienation of profits and of control by distant elites. It must be downplayed in the making of a locally inclusive “we” who can be imagined as sharing the wealth. This is a sleight of hand, a mystification in which local and global inequalities are covered up. In contrast, the anti-Kodeco faction has the advantages of a more ready-to-hand localism: Their goal is to preserve Meratus rights and forests. Yet they must conjure a transnational “we” to amplify this small cause with enough volume to speak. Translation across difference is key to both ways of achieving political voice—but with contrasting power dynamics.

原页 211, 212

Kodeco 辩论双方的政治，都涉及通过部署全套跨国资源来聚拢地方盟友。Kodeco 之所以获得中梅拉图斯山脉作为特许采伐区，是因为当被告知计划用其一块土地作集水区时，它威胁要在国际法院起诉（Chamin et al. 1999）。那些想保护森林的人也谈到国际背景，例如在吸引游客方面，正如一位发言人所说，“来自荷兰、澳大利亚、加拿大和美国”（Dinamika Berita 1999）。然而，跨国主义与地区动员的关系在双方那里有所不同。亲 Kodeco 派需要掩盖其跨国性，让参与者想象一种地方民粹主义。其跨国性提醒人们利润流向外部和远方精英的控制。在制造一个可以想象为共享财富的地方包容性“我们”时，这一点必须被淡化。这是障眼法，一种神秘化，地方与全球的不平等在其中被掩盖。相比之下，反 Kodeco 派拥有更为现成可用的地方主义优势：他们的目标是保护梅拉图斯人的权利和森林。然而他们必须召唤一个跨国“我们”，把这一小事业放大到足以发声的音量。跨越差异的翻译是两种获得政治声音的方式的关键——但权力动态截然不同。

原页 212

The Meratus Advocacy Alliance used translation to evoke a transnationally inclusive public who might jointly cherish the Meratus forest. For example, they argued that “the existence and holistic function of the Meratus Mountains conservation area, including biodiversity conservation, is very much tied to the life and death of many people (public interest) and the responsibility of the current generation to the next generation (intergenerational accountability)” (Aliansi Advokasi Meratus 2000: 5). The original statement is in Indonesian except for the words I have put in italics, which are in English. Indonesian is fully adequate to discuss public interest and intergenerational accountability. Translation, however, serves a political purpose, building an expansive public in the space between English and Indonesian. “Public interest” emerges in that space; the future to which generations look forward is simultaneously local, national, and global.

原页 212

梅拉图斯倡导联盟利用翻译，唤起一个可能共同珍视梅拉图斯森林的跨国包容性公众。例如，他们论证说：“梅拉图斯山脉保护区的存在与整体功能，包括生物多样性保护，与许多人的生死（public interest）以及当代人对下一代的责任（intergenerational accountability）密切相关”（Aliansi Advokasi Meratus 2000: 5）。原文陈述为印尼语，只有我用斜体标出的词为英语。印尼语完全足以讨论公共利益和代际责任。然而，翻译服务于一个政治目的，在英语与印尼语之间的空间里建构一个扩张性的公众。“公共利益”在那个空间中浮现；各代人展望的未来同时是地方的、国家的和全球的。

原页 212

In contrast, consider the governor’s words of encouragement to the proKodeco Meratus demonstrators. The provincial newspaper goes out of its way to point out that he addressed the demonstrators in the Banjar language (Banjarmasin Post, March 15, 2000). Banjar is the language of South Kalimantan’s regional majority. Meratus understand Banjar but have their own linguistic usages. The governor did not use Indonesian, the official language of the nation-state, but Banjar, the language identified with provincial populism. By including Meratus as if they were Banjar, he attempted to articulate populism—through translation. The newspaper’s readers gather that the demonstrators are being treated, respectfully, as the voice of the common people, the populace the government must support.2 Meanwhile, the newspaper reports Kodeco’s suspicion that anti-Kodeco sentiments are spread by outside agitators (ibid.). Who's in and who’s out? Where the antiKodeco faction must conjure virtual outsiders, the pro-Kodeco group must cover up its comprador status, while baselessly pointing fingers at the other guys.3

原页 212

相比之下，想想省长对亲 Kodeco 的梅拉图斯示威者的鼓励之词。省报特意指出，他用班贾尔语向示威者讲话（Banjarmasin Post，2000年3月15日）。班贾尔语是南加里曼丹地区多数人的语言。梅拉图斯人懂班贾尔语，但有自己的语言用法。省长没有使用印尼语——民族国家的官方语言——而是使用班贾尔语，一种与省级民粹主义相联系的语言。通过把梅拉图斯人包括进来，仿佛他们是班贾尔人，他试图通过翻译来表述民粹主义。报纸读者领会到，示威者被尊重地当作普通人民的声音，政府必须支持的民众。2与此同时，报纸报导 Kodeco 的怀疑：反 Kodeco 情绪是由外部煽动者散布的（同上）。谁在内，谁在外？反 Kodeco 派必须召唤虚拟的外部人，亲 Kodeco 集团则必须掩盖其买办地位，同时毫无根据地指责对方。3

原页 212

For both sides then, “voice” was built through intercultural practices, including translation. My job is to make these troublesome translations more apparent: to show that the coalitional structure of such engagements is not just a matter of adding allies, but also of remaking ideas, practices, and local, regional, and global histories. Only in this analytically symmetrical treatment can the differences between landscape destruction and the struggle for life shine through.

原页 212

因此，对双方来说，“声音”都是通过包括翻译在内的跨文化实践建构的。我的工作是让这些麻烦的翻译更加明显：表明此类参与的联盟结构不只是增加盟友，也是重造观念、实践以及地方、区域和全球历史。只有在这种分析上对称的处理中，地景破坏与争取生命的斗争之间的差异才能显现出来。

原页 213

Movements

原页 213

运动

原页 213
Beside the Potomac River,
at the house of George Washington
I encountered trees
that he planted.
Two hundred years from now
will you know
the tamarind trees I sowed?
—from Eka Budianta, “Houses of Love”1
原页 213
在波托马克河边，
在乔治·华盛顿的故居，
我遇见
他栽种的树。
两百年后，
你会知道
我播下的酸豆树吗？
——摘自埃卡·布迪安塔，《爱之屋》1
原页 213

movement. 1. A change of place or position; 2. A mental impulse, esp. one of desire or aversion; 3. An organization, coalition, or alliance of people working to advance a shared political, social, or artistic objective.2

原页 213

运动（movement）：1. 地点或位置的变化；2. 一种心理冲动，尤指欲望或厌恶的冲动；3. 为推进共同的政治、社会或艺术目标而工作的人群组织、联盟或同盟。2

原页 213

Travel changes the way we imagine our home places. We suddenly see them as fragile, strange, and worth savoring in new ways. In his poem “Houses of Love,” Eka Budianta (2000) is struck by the fragility of his tamarind trees as he readjusts time and space beneath George Washington’s trees by the Potomac River. All rural nature seems perishable in these times of cosmopolitan development. His solution—as in a number of Indonesian nature poems—is to move these cherished landscapes into his heart. After bringing us further on his travels through the blooming trees of a Tokyo spring, he returns to images of an Indonesian hillside. The poem ends with the bittersweet optimism of love and memory: “In the rainy city at the beginning of September, I have moved the bamboo house in which you were born into my heart for all time.”

原页 213

旅行改变我们想象家乡的方式。我们突然把它看作脆弱的、陌生的，值得以新方式品味。埃卡·布迪安塔（2000）在其诗作《爱之屋》中，在波托马克河边乔治·华盛顿的树下重新调整时间与空间时，被自己酸豆树的脆弱所触动。在这个世界主义发展的时代，一切乡村自然似乎都易朽。他的解决办法——正如许多印尼自然诗——是把这些珍爱的地景搬进心里。在带我们继续旅行、穿过东京春天开花的树木之后，他回到印尼山坡的意象。诗以爱与记忆的苦甜乐观作结：“在九月初的雨城，我已把你出生的竹屋永远搬进心里。”

原页 213, 214

The poet has moved, that is, “transferred” the rural landscape into his heart, an act only possible because of his own travels. In English the term “move” has more meanings to provoke us, and these are worth exploring. To move is to travel. To be moved is to open one’s heart. The travels of the poet stimulate his own heart’s movement. The landscape, re-visioned through travel, is transferred to become a moving personal commitment of love. Traveling ideas often stimulate us in just this way. We see the landscapes we know in relation to other places; we are moved to change how we think at both local and global scales. Social movements—including movements to preserve rural landscapes—grow from traveling forms of activism as well as the transformation of consciousness. This chapter shows how we might think of these two meanings together in analyzing global process: movement as mobility and movement as mobilization.

原页 213, 214

诗人已经移动，也就是说，把乡村地景“转移”进自己的心里；这一行为之所以可能，只因为他自己的旅行。英语中“move”有更多含义可供我们思考，值得探讨。To move 是旅行。To be moved 是敞开心扉。诗人的旅行激发他自己内心的运动。经过旅行重新审视的地景被转移，成为一种动人的个人爱的承诺。旅行的观念常常正是这样激发我们。我们参照其他地方来看待所熟悉的地景；我们被感动，在地方和全球尺度上改变思考方式。社会运动——包括保护乡村地景的运动——既生长于旅行的行动主义形式，也生长于意识的转变。本章展示在分析全球过程时，我们如何可以把运动的这两种含义放在一起思考：作为流动性的运动和作为动员的运动。

原页 214

What seems so simple to express in the poem, however, is not easy to explain as social science. Post-Cold War discussion of globalization glorified movement in the spread of liberalism, making the transnational travels of nongovernmental organizations, human rights advocacy, and civil society exemplars of an expanding freedom. This global movement was thought to remove layers of cultural superstition, distinction, and hierarchy to create a free—and frictionless—world. If freedom is the removal of obstructions, and movement is the fulfillment of individual desire, no mobilization is necessary.

原页 214

然而，诗里似乎如此容易表达的东西，作为社会科学却不容易解释。冷战后的全球化讨论在自由主义传播中颂扬运动，把非政府组织、人权倡导和公民社会的跨国旅行树为不断扩张的自由的典范。这种全球运动被认为将移除层层文化迷信、区分和等级，创造一个自由——且无摩擦——的世界。如果自由是移除障碍，运动是个体欲望的实现，那就无需动员。

原页 214

Critics of this perspective erect its mirror opposite: movement exemplifies the spread of unfreedom. Nongovernmental organizations, human rights advocacy, and civil society spread as a transnational governmentality, a new imperial power that reaches deeply into human souls. The new subjects of liberalism are even more trapped in power because they imagine it as freedom.3 Yet this vision shares presuppositions with liberalism’s boosters. Both agree that when liberalism spreads, it is completely successful in creating the subjects it conjures, for better or for worse. Liberalism’s dreams are no different than liberalism’s practice in these accounts.4

Motion can be imagined as creating a global regime, whether of freedom or governmentality, only to the extent that motion is imagined as loosening the grip of local practice. Yet the closer we examine social and geographical mobility, the less useful it seems to think in terms of overcoming such friction. This is where movement as mobility and mobilization can be of use. Movement helps us visualize forms of mobility with cultural and political definition—not just transcendent freedom. The specificity of the trajectory of movement is important for what results. Furthermore, there must be mobilization—the movement of the heart—for travel to remake the world. Mobilization refigures identities even as it draws from foreign connections and comparisons.

原页 214

这一视角的批评者竖起镜中的反面：运动例示了不自由的传播。非政府组织、人权倡导和公民社会作为跨国治理术传播，这是一种深入人类灵魂的新帝国权力。自由主义的新主体甚至更深地困在权力中，因为他们把权力想象为自由。3然而这一愿景与自由主义的吹捧者共享前提。两者都同意，当自由主义传播时，它完全成功地创造出它所召唤的主体，无论好坏。在这些叙述中，自由主义的梦想与自由主义的实践没有区别。4

只有当运动被想象为松开地方实践的掌控时，它才能被想象为创造一个全球体制，无论是自由的还是治理术的。然而我们越仔细审视社会与地理流动，从克服此类摩擦的角度思考就越显得无用。这正是作为流动性的运动与作为动员的运动可以派上用场之处。运动帮助我们想象具有文化与政治规定性的流动形式——而不只是超越性的自由。运动轨迹的特殊性对结果很重要。此外，旅行要重造世界，必须有动员——心灵的移动。动员在从外国联系与比较中汲取的同时，重新塑造身份。

原页 214, 215

To mobilize, a movement must offer a model of change in which individual activists as well as social groups can imagine themselves. The program must identify units of agency: What kinds of individuals and groups can make change? Two different answers organize this chapter, each keyed to the predicaments of a particular time. I first describe the careful interplay of nationalism and transnationalism under New Order repression and then turn to the mobilization of exuberant agency in the post-New Order moment of decentralization, in which ethnic, religious, and gender localizations direct a medley of transnational appropriations. In the first, the revitalized nation is the idealized agent of change; in the second, it is the charismatic package—the activist program itself—separated from national context. Each illustrates a way in which globally circulating terms, theories, and stories can be harnessed for local uses. Each requires a different model of analysis.

原页 214, 215

要动员，一场运动必须提供一种变革模型，让个体活动家和社会群体都能在其中想象自己。纲领必须界定能动性的单位：什么样的人和群体能够带来改变？两种不同的答案组织了本章，各自对应特定时刻的困境。我首先描述新秩序压制下民族主义与跨国主义之间小心翼翼的相互作用，然后转向新秩序后分权时刻充满活力的能动性动员，其中族群、宗教和性别的本地化引导着各种跨国挪用。在第一种情况下，重获活力的民族国家是理想化的变革主体；在第二种情况下，这一主体则是脱离国家语境、富有感召力的包裹——行动主义纲领本身。两者各自说明全球流通的术语、理论和故事如何能被套用于地方用途。两者各需要不同的分析模型。

原页 215

Under Indonesia’s New Order regime, the environmental movement struggled within what seemed an endless horizon of repression. Activists asked: How might a critical opposition be possible? Transnational networks were necessary, but only as they could be made relevant to the national problem of making space for criticism. In the context of this predicament, I trace the formation of a utopian nationalism that shadowed the state even as it attempted to refigure its possibilities. I explore how transnationalism was channeled into nationalism and imperial discipline corralled for utopian dreams.

原页 215

在印尼新秩序政权下，环保运动在似乎无尽的压抑地平线内挣扎。活动家问：批判性反对如何可能？跨国网络是必要的，但前提是它们能与在国内为批评开辟空间这一问题联系起来。在这种困境的背景下，我追踪一种乌托邦民族主义的形成，它与国家如影随形，同时试图重新塑造其可能性。我探究跨国主义如何被导入民族主义，帝国规训如何被圈起来服务于乌托邦梦想。

原页 215

After the fall of the New Order, the nation entered a hopeful but chaotic period of reform. Political causes moved to the provinces as decentralization became a national agenda. In this moment of openness, activists considered how disenfranchised people might be mobilized to fight for their rights. They turned for precedence to transnational initiatives—and without the urgent necessity of national translations. In the jumbled creativity of turn-of-the-century Indonesia, transnational stories ricocheted here and there providing fodder for alternative dreams. Al Qaeda competed with Bollywood and Marx in shaping local visions. In this context, I trace the travels of new utopian visions. How do political models from elsewhere become relevant? Indonesia as a nation is no longer my focus; regional, ethnic, and gender dynamics come into view. Yet locations matter. Mobility means nothing without mobilization. My story retells other traveling stories, attentive to their situated uses and revisions.

原页 215

新秩序倒台后，国家进入一个充满希望却混乱的改革时期。随着分权成为国家议程，政治事业转向各省。在这个开放时刻，活动家考虑如何动员被剥夺权利的人为自身权利而斗争。他们转向跨国倡议寻求先例——此时不再迫切需要把它们转译到国家层面。在世纪之交印尼的杂乱创造力中，跨国故事四处弹跳，为另类梦想提供素材。基地组织与宝莱坞和马克思竞争，塑造地方愿景。在这种背景下，我追踪新乌托邦愿景的旅行。来自别处的政治模型如何变得相关？印尼作为一个国家不再是我的焦点；地区、族群和性别动态进入视野。然而地点很重要。没有动员，流动性毫无意义。我的故事重述其他旅行的故事，关注它们的情境化使用与修订。

原页 215

In the light of these contrasts, I offer two kinds of tellings. First I explore the contradictions of liberalism as developed by brave—and privileged—critics of an authoritarian regime. Here, utopian dreams and disciplinary regimes beckon to each other, remaking the possibilities of freedom. Rather than beginning as most critics do with the contamination of utopian nationalism by privilege, discipline, and colonial discourse, I show how one might glimpse the movement's possibilities—without forgetting its limits.

原页 215

鉴于这些对比，我提供两种讲述。首先，我探究威权政权那些勇敢——且享有特权——的批评者所发展的自由主义及其内在矛盾。在这里，乌托邦梦想与规训体制彼此召唤，重造自由的可能性。我不像大多数批评者那样从乌托邦民族主义被特权、规训和殖民话语污染开始，而是展示人们如何可以瞥见运动的各种可能性——同时不忘记其局限。

原页 215, 216

In my second set of stories, activism has taken advantage of the confusions and openings of a time of reform. Regional, religious, and gender initiatives reach out to harvest allegorical packages as they zip around the globe, unmoored from their origins. Here too there is a model for understanding movement: utopian critique is commodified in allegorical packages. Scholars have had difficulty in imagining how to trace traveling forms of politics; the two most available models, national history and global circulation, territorialize and universalize, respectively, each erasing travel. My story lays out one strategy for showing how close and distant productions of politics intertwine. Together, the parts of the chapter detail varied possibilities of enmeshing mobility and mobilization.

原页 215, 216

在我的第二组故事中，行动主义利用了改革时代的混乱与开口。地区、宗教和性别倡议伸手收获寓言包裹，这些包裹在全球飞驰，脱离其起源。这里也有一个理解运动的模型：乌托邦批评被商品化为寓言包裹。学者难以想象如何追踪旅行的政治形式；最现成的两种模型——国家史与全球流通——分别领土化和普遍化，各自抹去了旅行。我的故事提出一种策略，展示近处与远处的政治生产如何交织在一起。本章各部分合起来，详述把流动性与动员交织起来的多种可能。

原页 216

Where Dreams Shadow Discipline

原页 216

梦想与规训如影随形之处

原页 216

To many scholars, the nation is obsolete, a worn shoe discarded in the race toward globalization. Yet the nation continues to be a key site for political struggle.5 In late New Order Indonesia, radical politics was nationalist politics. It was also self-consciously transnational. Nationalism and transnationalism were intertwined in forming dreams of social change.6

There are many reasons not to trust nationalist visions. Nationalisms have worked hand in hand with racism and coercive state power. Meanwhile, transnational politics sponsors its own coercive disciplines, forcing its categories and priorities on to reluctant nationalists. It is not easy to create a radical politics between the two.

原页 216

对许多学者来说，民族国家已经过时，是在奔向全球化的竞赛中被丢弃的破鞋。然而民族国家仍然是政治斗争的关键场所。5在新秩序晚期的印尼，激进政治就是民族主义政治。它也是自觉的跨国政治。民族主义与跨国主义在形成社会变革梦想时交织在一起。6

有许多理由不信任民族主义愿景。民族主义曾与种族主义和强制国家权力携手合作。与此同时，跨国政治推行自身的强制性规训，把其范畴和优先事项强加给不情愿的民族主义者。要在两者之间创造激进政治并不容易。

原页 216

Yet in the 1980s and 1990s, Indonesian activists built something rather exciting under the banner of environmentalism.7 This was a time of state repression. The environment was one of the few topics open for critical discussion. Environmentalism cleared the way for other movements in the 1990s, blossoming into human rights and labor concerns, as these became possible. In its time, it was one of the most significant players in building a democratic opposition to an autocratic regime. Drawing heavily from transnational sources of funding and legitimacy, the movement worked to create a counterculture to coercive state development. In resource-rich rural areas, development meant state expansion and the expropriation of land and natural resources. Environmentalism created an alternative, however fragile. Rural community leaders were offered a new set of urban interlocutors; campaigns for local and customary rights multiplied. Global and national disciplines notwithstanding, it is hard for me not to be thrilled at the liveliness and idealism of the environmental movement of this period.

原页 216

然而在20世纪80和90年代，印尼活动家在环保主义旗帜下建设了一些相当激动人心的东西。7这是一个国家压制的时代。环境是少数开放给批判性讨论的话题之一。环保主义为20世纪90年代的其他运动清出道路，随着条件允许，进一步发展到人权与劳工议题。在它的时代，它是建立对专制政权民主反对的最重要参与者之一。这场运动大量汲取跨国资金与合法性来源，努力创造一种对抗强制性国家发展的反文化。在资源丰富的乡村地区，发展意味着国家扩张以及对土地和自然资源的征用。环保主义创造了一种替代，尽管脆弱。乡村社群领袖有了一批新的城市对话者；争取地方和习惯权利的运动成倍增加。尽管有全球与国家层面的规训，我很难不为这一时期环保运动的活力与理想主义感到激动。

原页 216

What are the forms of attention that might allow us to track the excitement of this case? We cannot focus only on traveling disciplines; we must also attend to how movements mobilize. What are the sources of passion here?

原页 216

什么样的关注形式能让我们追踪这个案例的激动之处？我们不能只关注流动的规训；我们还必须关注运动如何动员。这里的激情来源是什么？

原页 216, 217

Northern readers expect environmentalism to mean the protection of wilderness or endangered species. This is not a good place to start, although these goals have not gone missing in Indonesia. Instead, the movement has been most concerned with threats to human landscapes, such as pollution, destructive development, or the theft of forests from rural communities. Indonesian environmentalism is and has been heterogeneous. I am most interested here in the prominent strand of the movement that became marked with a radical social populism. Indonesian environmental populism contrasts sharply with the elitism of many northern conservationists, and it facilitates the types of rural alliances that have not been possible in the global north. This populist strand was shaped by the goal of building a national coalition against state repression during the period of New Order rule.8

原页 216, 217

北方读者期待环保主义意味着保护荒野或濒危物种。这不是一个好的起点，尽管这些目标在印尼并未消失。相反，这场运动最关心的是对人类地景的威胁，如污染、破坏性发展，或从乡村社群手中盗走森林。印尼环保主义现在是、曾经也是异质的。我最感兴趣的是运动中以激进的社会民粹主义为特征的那一突出脉络。印尼环保民粹主义与许多北方保护主义者的精英主义形成鲜明对比，它促成了全球北方未能形成的那类乡村联盟。这条民粹主义脉络是由新秩序统治时期建立反国家压制全国联盟的目标塑造的。8

原页 217

To make global movement matter for the nation: This was the goal for many environmentalists in Indonesia in the 1980s and 1990s. Environmental damage was both global and national, just as development, while a transnational project, was channeled by the state. Similarly environmental protection: Even as activists were inspired by transnational activism, they wanted a national movement to protect the environment. Saving the nation and saving the environment became linked causes. Yet activism could not prosper independently of the state. Only by working inside and around state forms could activists imagine alternatives to state-sponsored environmental destruction.

原页 217

让全球运动对国家有意义：这是20世纪80和90年代许多印尼环保主义者的目标。环境破坏既是全球的也是国家的，正如发展虽然是一个跨国项目，却由国家引导。环境保护也是如此：即使活动家受到跨国行动主义启发，他们想要一场保护环境的全国运动。拯救国家与拯救环境成为相互联系的事业。然而，行动主义不能独立于国家而繁荣。只有通过在国家形式内部及其周围运作，活动家才能想象国家赞助的环境破坏之外的替代方案。

原页 217

The Indonesian environmental movement prospered in part because certain technocrats within the state bureaucracy supported it. The New Order had come to power on the promise of Indonesian modernity, with transnational law, science, and business standards in high regard. Indonesian representatives to the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm in 1972 came home with enthusiastic prescriptions for environmental reform. By 1978, the state had installed a Ministry of Population and Environment, and in 1982 the Basic Environmental Management Act established Indonesians’ rights to a clean and healthy environment. Environmental Study Centers were established at state universities. The nongovernmental organizations that came into being in the 1980s owed their sense of promise and their freedom of maneuver to this state sponsorship, and particularly to a few prominent bureaucrats who nurtured and protected them, building their own constituencies in the process.9

原页 217

印尼环保运动之所以繁荣，部分是因为国家官僚机构内某些技术官僚支持它。新秩序是靠印尼现代化的承诺上台的，高度重视跨国法律、科学和商业标准。1972年参加斯德哥尔摩联合国人类环境会议的印尼代表，带着对环境改革的热情处方回国。到1978年，国家设立了人口与环境部；1982年，《基本环境管理法》确立了印尼人享有清洁健康环境的权利。国立大学设立了环境研究中心。20世纪80年代出现的非政府组织，把希望感和回旋自由归功于这种国家赞助，尤其归功于几位培育和保护它们的著名官僚；这些官僚也在此过程中建立了自己的支持群体。9

原页 217, 218

Environmental activists came out of the universities into a world of expanded options for young urban professionals and managers. New Order wealth allowed this class to grow exponentially. The children of this new prosperity swelled NGO ranks, creating less bureaucratic forms of public service, even as some bureaucrats feared and controlled their independence.10 And this ambivalence was reproduced among the rising group of environmental advocates. Some developed the technical and bureaucratic solutions possible within the government. Others made issues of social and environmental justice central to their ideals. Drawing on Indonesian legacies of populism, they advocated for grassroots causes. Their organizations formulated a development counterculture, with its own claims to national legitimacy. Their structured groups and policy plans closely shadowed the state, offering alternatives even as the state’s national objectives were in many ways reproduced. Meanwhile, this counterculture flourished because during the same period transnational donor organizations began to channel their funds through nongovernmental organizations around the world. In the late 1980s, Indonesian environmental organizations found themselves rich with funding and support. Dozens of groups were formed across the political spectrum. As one activist explained to me, reading a roster of environmental groups in the late 1980s it was difficult to distinguish the radical critics from the president’s cronies.

原页 217, 218

环保活动家从大学出来，进入一个年轻城市专业人士和管理者选择扩展的世界。新秩序的财富让这个阶级指数式增长。这种新繁荣的子女充实了非政府组织队伍，创造了较少官僚化的公共服务形式，即使一些官僚恐惧并控制它们的独立性。10这种矛盾心理在崛起的环保倡导者群体中也被复制。一些人发展出政府内部可能的技术与官僚解决方案。另一些人把社会与环境正义议题置于理想的核心。他们借鉴印尼民粹主义遗产，倡导基层事业。他们的组织构想出一种发展反文化，有其自身的国家合法性主张。他们的组织化团体和政策方案紧随国家的形式，提供替代方案，即使国家的全国目标在许多方面被复制。与此同时，这种反文化之所以繁荣，是因为同一时期跨国捐助组织开始通过世界各地的非政府组织输送资金。20世纪80年代末，印尼环保组织发现自己资金和支持充裕。政治光谱的各个位置都出现了团体，总计数十个。正如一位活动家向我解释，读着20世纪80年代末环保团体的名册，很难把激进批评者与总统的亲信区分开来。

原页 218

Many of the most important environmental advocacy groups of the 1980s and 1990s centered themselves in Jakarta, the national capital. From there, they coordinated causes and campaigns that reached across the nation. WALHI (Wahana Lingkungan Hidup Indonesia), the Indonesian Environmental Forum, achieved a particular importance as a national umbrella group.11 WALHI coordinated a host of specialized member groups as well as regional fora representing each of Indonesia’s provinces. WALHI included national groups working on specialized issues (e.g., forests, pesticides, climate change) as well as rural community activists and provincial nature lovers. National coordination made it possible for a variety of activists to bring their causes to a wide audience and to seek national solutions.12

原页 218

20世纪80和90年代许多最重要的环保倡导团体都以首都雅加达为中心。从那里，它们协调遍及全国的事业与运动。WALHI（Wahana Lingkungan Hidup Indonesia，印尼环境论坛）作为全国性伞状组织获得了特别重要的地位。11WALHI 协调众多专门会员团体以及代表印尼各省的地区论坛。WALHI 既包括处理专门议题（如森林、农药、气候变化）的全国性团体，也包括乡村社群活动家和省级自然爱好者。全国协调使各种活动家能够把自己的事业带给广泛受众，并寻求全国性解决方案。12

原页 218

What was radical about this nationalism? Under the New Order, mass protests were suppressed; electoral competition meant little. Radical politics emerged as utopian critique; its goal was to raise political expectations. It questioned the inevitability of state coercion and documented the excesses of state and corporate greed. Occasionally, it was possible to change a policy; most often the goals were a longer-term transformation of public consciousness. Activists were thrilled when, even in failure, their campaigns caused people to think.

原页 218

这种民族主义的激进之处何在？新秩序下，群众抗议被压制；选举竞争意义甚微。激进政治作为乌托邦批评出现；其目标是提高政治期待。它质疑国家强制的不可避免性，记录国家和企业贪婪的过度行为。偶尔有可能改变某项政策；最常见的目标是公众意识的长期转变。当运动即使在失败中也促使人们思考时，活动家会感到激动。

原页 218, 219

Raising political expectations was made possible by finding a critical edge between transnational and national positions. Activists found transnational standards to criticize national policies; they articulated national priorities to refocus transnational initiatives. In this play of here and there, three kinds of tactics stand out. First, liberal initiatives could be used against liberal institutions: New Order pretensions of transnationally acceptable democratic standards were challenged by taking liberalism seriously. Second, discussion within the movement about the partial successes of their own campaigns sharpened awareness about the possibilities and limitations of political coalitions at home and abroad. Third, self-conscious practices of translation focused attention on the making of a national voice. Linguistic interfaces formed sites for debating alternative visions, domesticating the foreign, and synthesizing new forms of national pluralism. Each of these tactics incorporates transnational disciplinary standards into the very techniques of national liberation. At the same time, each enlarges the confining enclosures of these disciplines to make hope possible. My next sections illustrate the conundrums of each of these three tactics.

原页 218, 219

提高政治期待之所以可能，是因为在跨国与国家立场之间找到了一条批判性的边缘。活动家找到跨国标准来批评国家政策；他们阐述国家优先事项以重新聚焦跨国倡议。在这种此处与彼处的运作中，有三种策略尤为突出。第一，自由主义的倡议可以被用来反对自由主义的制度：通过认真对待自由主义，挑战新秩序自称符合跨国认可的民主标准的说辞。第二，运动内部关于自身运动部分成功的讨论，加深了对国内外政治联盟可能性与局限的认识。第三，自觉的翻译实践把注意力集中在民族声音的制造上。语言接口成为辩论另类愿景、驯化外来物、综合新形式的国家多元主义的场所。这些策略每一种都把跨国规训标准纳入民族解放的技术本身。同时，每一种都扩大这些规训的限制性围栏，使希望成为可能。我接下来的几节说明这三种策略各自的难题。

原页 219

Using Liberalism Against Itself

原页 219

以自由主义反制自由主义自身

原页 219

A 1994 courtroom vigil concretized my respect for the energy of activists working jointly for environment and nation—as it also reminded me of the specificity of this agenda. Activists had won a small victory when a sympathetic Supreme Court judge ruled that a group of villagers whose land had been flooded by the Kedung Ombo dam deserved more compensation. It was expected that—as indeed happened—this ruling would soon be overturned.13 But before this return to the status quo, activists could use the ruling to call upon the state to live up to its promises. Adding this duty into their overextended schedules, activists entered the courtroom every morning at 8 A.M. to remind the world that justice had not yet been done. They didn’t expect to win; the vigil would only prick the conscience of the nation. The vigil urged everyone to ask, Is the legal system real?

原页 219

1994年的一次法庭守候，让我对同时为环境与国家而工作的活动家的能量产生具体的敬意——它也提醒我这一议程的特殊性。活动家赢得了一次小胜利：一位同情他们的最高法院法官裁定，土地被克东翁博（Kedung Ombo）大坝淹没的一群村民应得到更多补偿。人们预料这项裁决会很快被推翻——事实也确实如此。13但在回归现状之前，活动家可以利用这项裁决呼吁国家履行承诺。活动家把这一职责加入他们已过度排满的日程，每天上午8点进入法庭，提醒世界正义尚未实现。他们不指望获胜；守候只会刺痛民族的良心。守候促使每个人问：法律体系是真的吗？

原页 219

The use of liberalism to disturb the assurance of what was supposed to be a liberal state was especially apparent in movement encounters with the legal system.14 Many environmental organizations worked hard to build a national culture of law in Indonesia. By the late 1980s, Indonesia had a number of strongly worded environmental laws; however, these laws did very little to nurture a healthy environment as long as they were never enforced. Environmentalists wanted to vitalize the legal system, to make it useful and accountable to Indonesian citizens rather than a state showcase for international relations. They hoped to push the state to live up to its laws and to inform citizens that they should make these laws their own.

原页 219

利用自由主义来搅扰一个本应是自由主义国家的自信，在运动与法律体系的交锋中尤为明显。14许多环保组织努力在印尼建设一种全国性的法治文化。到20世纪80年代末，印尼已有若干措辞强硬的环境法；然而，只要从不执行，这些法律就几乎无助于培育健康的环境。环保主义者想激活法律体系，使之有用、对印尼公民负责，而不是国家在国际关系中的展示橱窗。他们希望推动国家遵守自己的法律，并告知公民应当把这些法律变成自己的。

原页 219, 220

Law seemed a site of possibility for expanding national consciousness in part because it was an allowable arena of discussion. Law had a special position under the New Order.15 From the start, lawyers were important supporters of the regime, and the regime supported law. The Old Order had toyed with “revolutionary law,” a system that allowed judges to decide, without regard for precedent, in the interest of the people. Lawyers were outraged, and they turned with enthusiasm to the New Order's promises to uphold consistent legal standards. The New Order's encouragement of international business also opened opportunities for lawyers. In this privileged position, a few lawyers were able to form an early and persistent source of criticism of New Order policy. In the 1980s and 1990s, Lembaga Bantuan Hukum or Legal Aid Foundations, known as LBH, formed a site for discussion of issues of inequality and justice. Through joint campaigns and lawsuits, many environmental activists directed their activism to questions of law.

原页 219, 220

法律似乎是一个扩展民族意识的可能场所，部分因为它是一个允许讨论的领域。法律在新秩序下享有特殊地位。15从一开始，律师就是该政权的重要支持者，政权也支持法律。旧秩序曾尝试推行“革命法”，这种制度允许法官不顾先例，为人民利益作决定。律师们大为愤怒，转而热情地支持新秩序维护一致法律标准的承诺。新秩序对国际商业的鼓励也为律师打开了机会。在这一特权位置上，少数律师得以形成对新秩序政策早期而持久的批评来源。20世纪80和90年代，法律援助基金会（Lembaga Bantuan Hukum，简称 LBH）成为讨论不平等与正义议题的场所。通过联合运动和诉讼，许多环保活动家把行动主义转向法律问题。

原页 220

In 1986 and 1987, for example, laws were passed requiring environmental impact assessments and forming implementation guidelines. But environmental impact assessments are justifications for development unless public pressure is brought to bear on assessors to consider social and environmental problems. Environmentalists wanted to make it possible for ordinary citizens to participate in the process (WALHI 1993). WALHI organized “barefoot clinics” to train community people to make a difference in environmental assessment.

原页 220

例如，1986年和1987年通过了要求环境影响评估并制定实施指南的法律。但环境影响评估不过是发展的辩护理由，除非对评估者施加公众压力，使其考虑社会与环境问题。环保主义者希望使普通公民有可能参与这一过程（WALHI 1993）。WALHI 组织“赤脚诊所”，培训社群民众在环境评估中发挥作用。

原页 220, 221

Besides training programs, there were lawsuits. Perhaps the most well known was WALHI’s 1988 suit, pursued jointly with the national LBH, to hold the Indorayon Company (P. T. Inti Indorayon) responsible for the environmental damage the company inflicted on the Lake Toba region of Sumatra. The company was destroying the area’s forests to supply raw materials for making rayon in a pulp mill. Local residents used these forests for grazing and forest products, and they protested against having their land stolen as well as against the eucalyptus plantations with which the company replaced the forests. Meanwhile, the factory was polluting the air and water. Environmentalists’ challenge to Indorayon raised issues of environmental damage in a context in which activists could also talk about social justice—as well as crony capitalism, official corruption, and popular resistance. WALHI's suit argued that the company had not conducted a proper environmental impact assessment. WALHI lost, but the suit was a victory in establishing the right of NGOs to sue on behalf of the environment (WALHI and YLBHI 1993).16

Lawsuits were an arena in which victory meant raising national consciousness rather than winning in court. The most striking example of this is WALHI’s 1994 joint lawsuit against then-president Suharto, for giving an interest-free loan from the national reforestation fund to his close crony (and successor), Habibie, to finance his aircraft factory (Indonesian Center for Environmental Law 1994). The reforestation fund was a tax established on commercial logging and intended to support tree planting and management. It was especially bold for activists to object at this moment, because the government was closing down political expression. National magazines had been closed—for reporting critically on Habibie. The president had distributed draft guidelines for NGOs that would require them to relinquish political commentary if they received money from abroad; no one was sure the NGO community could survive. The suit was impossible; the courts refused to hear it. But assembling the suit was an organizing action, and it powerfully intertwined issues of democracy and environmental well-being.

原页 220, 221

除培训项目外，还有诉讼。最著名的也许是 WALHI 1988年的诉讼，它与全国性 LBH 共同提起，要求 Indorayon 公司（P. T. Inti Indorayon）对公司在苏门答腊多巴湖地区造成的环境破坏负责。该公司毁坏该地区森林，为浆粕厂制造人造丝提供原料。当地居民利用这些森林放牧和采集林产品，他们抗议土地被夺走，也抗议公司用以替代森林的桉树种植园。与此同时，工厂污染空气和水。环保主义者对 Indorayon 的挑战在活动家也能谈论社会正义的语境中提出了环境破坏问题——还有裙带资本主义、官员腐败和民众抵抗。WALHI 的诉讼主张公司未进行适当的环境影响评估。WALHI 败诉，但该诉讼在确立非政府组织代环境起诉的权利方面是一场胜利（WALHI and YLBHI 1993）。16

诉讼是一个竞技场，其中胜利意味着提高民族意识，而不是在法庭上获胜。最引人注目的例子是 WALHI 1994年对时任总统苏哈托的联合诉讼，因为他从国家造林基金中给亲密亲信（也是继任者）哈比比提供无息贷款，资助其飞机制造厂（Indonesian Center for Environmental Law 1994）。造林基金是对商业伐木征收的税，旨在支持植树和管理。活动家在这一时刻提出异议尤其大胆，因为政府正在关闭政治表达空间。全国性杂志已被查封——因为批评性地报道哈比比。总统分发了非政府组织指导草案，要求接受国外资金的非政府组织放弃政治评论；没有人确定非政府组织界能否存活。这场诉讼毫无胜算；法院拒绝审理。但组织这场诉讼本身就是一项组织行动，它有力地交织了民主与环境福祉的议题。

原页 221

Stirring Up Debate

原页 221

激起辩论

原页 221

Not everyone in the movement liked the priority of legal strategies. In the campaign against the Kedung Ombo dam, mentioned earlier, many activists argued in hindsight that too close a dependence on the law delayed the initiation of other strategies of protest, closed the political imagination, and formed part of the movement’s terrible reliance on technical and anti-democratic solutions. Debates about politics, such as that which followed the Kedung Ombo campaign, were an invigorating part of the environmental struggle, allowing participants to reexamine their premises, and thus expanding the range of critique.

原页 221

运动中并非所有人都喜欢法律策略的优先地位。在先前提到的反对克东翁博大坝的运动中，许多活动家事后认为，过于依赖法律延误了其他抗议策略的启动，封闭了政治想象，并构成运动对技术和反民主解决方案的可怕依赖的一部分。关于政治的辩论，例如克东翁博运动之后的辩论，是环境斗争中令人振奋的部分，让参与者重新审视自己的前提，从而扩大批评的范围。

原页 221

Official New Order models of social harmony had a very limited tolerance for political debate. Censorship was expected, and the sporadic punishment of public critics kept everyone feeling cautious. The dampening of public political discussion limited alliances across social sectors, isolating each group in their own caution. The promise of the environmental movement was its ability to bring together urban and rural critics of coercive development by using the strength of the alliance between foreign and domestic environmentalism. Yet the question remained: Would these coalitions reinforce power differences or overcome them in a new solidarity?

原页 221

新秩序官方关于社会和谐的模型对政治辩论的容忍非常有限。审查是可以预期的，对公开批评者的零星惩罚让每个人都保持谨慎。公共政治讨论的压抑限制了跨社会部门的联盟，把每个群体隔离在各自的谨慎中。环保运动的希望在于，它能够利用国外与国内环保主义联盟的力量，把对强制发展持批评态度的城乡批评者团结起来。然而问题依然存在：这些联盟会强化权力差异，还是在新的团结中克服它们？

原页 221

The campaign against the Kedung Ombo dam concentrated both hopes and fears about environmentalist solidarity. A review of the events illustrates the paradoxes that formed the heart of national discussion.

原页 221

反对克东翁博大坝的运动集中了对环保团结的希望与恐惧。回顾这些事件，可以说明构成全国讨论核心的悖论。

原页 221, 222

Peasant mobilization was slow to begin, exclusively channeled into legalism at first, and only belatedly picked up by protesters. The Kedung Ombo dam project, financed by the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank, and Exim Bank of Japan, was designed in the 1970s to provide irrigation, control floods, and generate electrical power. Some 37 villages containing up to 30,000 people would be displaced by the dam’s reservoir.17 In 1986, villagers were called together by officials and ordered to join the government's transmigration program, which would resettle them outside Java.18 Small amounts of monetary compensation were offered to landowners, but not enough to buy other land. Threats were made against them if they did not cooperate. Yet despite promises and threats, a core group of villagers was unwilling to leave. The Kedung Ombo campaign revolved around the stubborn refusal of these villagers to move, even when the waters began rising in 1989.

原页 221, 222

农民动员开始缓慢，起初完全被导入法律主义，抗议者直到很晚才接手。克东翁博水坝项目由世界银行、亚洲开发银行和日本进出口银行资助，设计于20世纪70年代，旨在提供灌溉、控制洪水和发电。约37个村庄、多达3万人将因水库而流离失所。171986年，官员召集村民，命令他们参加政府的移民项目，该项目将把他们重新安置到爪哇以外。18向土地所有者提供了少量金钱补偿，但不足以购买其他土地。如果他们不合作，便施以威胁。然而尽管有承诺和威胁，一群核心村民仍不愿离开。克东翁博运动围绕这些村民的顽固拒绝迁走而展开，即使1989年水位开始上涨。

原页 222

The villagers’ first and most important strategy was to try to exact fair compensation for their land. Fair compensation seemed a reasonable demand: First, LBH legal activists promoted this strategy and were willing to put their time into it.19 Second, the demand for compensation was becoming a form of New Order “common sense,” popularizing the regime’s rhetoric of commoditization. The kinds of demands activists later raised—that the dam should not be built, or that the government should consult people before moving them—would have been difficult. Yet the legalism of the fair compensation battle had drawbacks even beyond its weak utopianism: competing sources of advocacy, a separation between landowners and landless, and what one commentator called a “wait-and-see attitude” that delayed other efforts (Rumansara 1998: 131).

原页 222

村民最初也是最重要的策略，是设法为土地争取公平补偿。公平补偿似乎是合理要求：第一，LBH 法律活动家推动这一策略，并愿意投入时间。19第二，补偿要求正在成为新秩序“常识”的一种形式，普及了该政权的商品化修辞。活动家后来提出的那类要求——不应修建大坝，或者政府应在迁移民众之前征询他们的意见——会很难。然而，公平补偿之争的法律主义除了其薄弱的乌托邦主义之外还有缺陷：相互竞争的倡导力量、土地所有者与无地者之间的分离，以及一位评论者所谓拖延其他努力的“观望态度”（Rumansara 1998: 131）。

原页 222

The moment of common cause was full of misunderstanding. Foreign NGO activists organized a different kind of campaign. An international NGO consortium focusing on Indonesia formed in 1985 and took up the cause. Northern NGOs (e.g., the Environmental Defense Fund, the International Rivers Network) publicized the issue and offered their criticisms of the dam to the World Bank. Southern NGO networks were also important; activists worked through the Malaysia-based Asia-Pacific Peoples Environmental Network and were in contact with Indian activists mobilizing to stop India’s Narmada Valley dams. This was the period in which opposition to big dams from many countries became coordinated as an international anti-dam movement. Indonesian activists played a role in this consolidation.

原页 222

共同事业的那一刻充满误解。外国非政府组织活动家组织了另一种运动。一个关注印尼的国际非政府组织联盟于1985年成立并接过了这项事业。北方非政府组织（例如环境保护基金、国际河流网络）宣传该问题，并向世界银行提出对大坝的批评。南方非政府组织网络也很重要；活动家通过总部设在马来西亚的亚太人民环境网络开展工作，并与动员阻止印度纳尔默达河谷大坝的印度活动家保持联系。这一时期，来自许多国家反对大坝的反对派协调成为一场国际反坝运动。印尼活动家在这场整合中发挥了作用。

原页 222, 223

Meanwhile, students began to protest. The press took notice. As the flooding began, a Solidarity Group for the Victims of Kedung Ombo formed to raise issues of government corruption, due process, and human rights. A charismatic Catholic priest turned attention to the plight of the children whose homes were being flooded. Delegations of villagers and students complained to various sectors of the government. The campaign drew national attention and raised a lot of discussion. But as one activist group put it, “Comments, both from supporters and enemies of the people are not enough. Definitely, the people are waiting for solutions” (SKEPHI 1991: 29).

Relations among the different sectors of the campaign were never smooth. Their goals diverged: The villagers wanted fair compensation for the land. The students wanted a democratic and just government. Transnational NGOs wanted to stop the ecological destruction of big dams. These goals clashed even as they found a moment of convergence. Time was short, with few chances to forge mutual accommodations. Disagreements formed problems in the coordination of the campaign. Yet the creativity of the movement also flourished through these differences. The campaign did not rely on precedent; it had to form its own connections. That these were rough and makeshift speaks to their power as well as their limitations: They made a new kind of protest possible.

原页 222, 223

与此同时，学生开始抗议。媒体注意到了。当洪水开始上涨时，克东翁博受害者团结小组成立，提出政府腐败、正当程序和人权问题。一位有魅力的天主教神父把注意力转向家园被淹的儿童的困境。村民和学生代表团向政府各部门投诉。这场运动引起全国关注，引发大量讨论。但正如一个活动家团体所说：“来自人民支持者和敌人的评论都不够。显然，人民在等待解决方案”（SKEPHI 1991: 29）。

运动各个参与群体之间的关系从未顺畅。他们的目标分歧：村民想要土地的公平补偿。学生想要一个民主公正的政府。跨国非政府组织想阻止大坝的生态破坏。这些目标相互冲突，即使在它们找到汇合时刻时也是如此。时间短暂，鲜有机会达成相互妥协。分歧构成了运动协调中的问题。然而运动的创造力也通过这些差异蓬勃发展。这场运动不依赖先例；它必须形成自己的连接。这些连接粗糙而临时，既说明其力量也说明其局限：它们使一种新型抗议成为可能。

原页 223

Ad hoc tactics are undemocratic. The previous assessment celebrates contingency in the coalescence of the movement, but it also invites substantive criticism. Activist and analyst George Aditjondro is the most damning. He concludes one discussion of the Kedong Ombo protests as follows: “Apart from its class bias, Indonesian anti-dam struggles have brought the extraparliamentary, patron-mediated, ad hoc and Java-centric nature of Indonesian politics to the fore” (1998: 47). His review of the campaign stresses the role of dissatisfied army officers in supporting the alliance between students and farmers, allowing mass demonstrations and media coverage to continue even though they were prohibited by law. Political patrons—such as Environmental Minister Emil Salim—changed their positions as the regime’s winds blew. When activists took their struggle to an international NGO conference, which forwarded a petition of complaints about the dam to the World Bank, President Suharto retaliated against the NGOs, causing a retreat to more conservative strategies. Meanwhile, the movement depended on experts, intellectuals, and the media. “[T]he history of anti-dam struggles in Indonesia is a history of reinforcing global expertocracy instead of strengthening institutions of participatory and direct democracy” (1998: 48). Aditjondro’s sharp criticisms were among the most important in stirring debate and reassessment in the 1990s.20

The campaign’s successes were largely symbolic. Despite the campaign, the dam was completed and brought into operation. Because of the campaign, resettlement options for displaced villagers widened. Some were offered land in nearby national forests. Others have been allowed to farm illegally in the greenbelt established to protect the dam.21 Yet it would be difficult to claim that justice has been achieved for the poor.

原页 223
