临时策略是不民主的。前文的评估赞美运动汇合中的偶然性，但它也招致实质性批评。活动家兼分析者乔治·阿迪琼德罗（George Aditjondro）的批评最为严厉。他这样结束关于克东翁博抗议的一场讨论：“除了其阶级偏见之外，印尼反坝斗争还凸显了印尼政治中议会外的、由庇护人中介的、临时的和以爪哇为中心的性质”（1998: 47）。他对运动的回顾强调不满的军官在支持学生与农民联盟中的作用，使大规模示威和媒体报道得以继续，尽管它们被法律禁止。政治庇护人——如环境部长埃米尔·萨利姆——随着政权风向改变立场。当活动家把斗争带到一场国际非政府组织会议，会议向世界银行转交了一份关于大坝的投诉请愿书，苏哈托总统对非政府组织进行报复，导致退回更保守的策略。与此同时，运动依赖专家、知识分子和媒体。“印尼反坝斗争的历史，是一部强化全球专家统治而非加强参与式民主和直接民主制度的历史”（1998: 48）。阿迪琼德罗尖锐的批评是20世纪90年代激起辩论与重新评估的最重要批评之一。20

运动的成功在很大程度上是象征性的。尽管有运动，大坝还是完工并投入运行。因为运动，流离失所村民的重新安置选择扩大了。一些人获得附近国有林中的土地。另一些人被允许在保护大坝的绿化带中非法耕作。21然而很难宣称穷人已经获得正义。

原页 223

Instead, the major impact of the campaign has been in changing the symbolic valence of dam building. Big dams are symbols of human mastery over nature; they are among the most high-profile international development packages. In the second half of the twentieth century, big dams became a standard of national sovereignty. Every nation wanted its own dams, and multilateral development banks wanted every nation to have them.22 In Indonesia in the 1970s and 1980s, big dams were seen as monuments of national development.23 Opposing them hit a nerve.

原页 223

相反，运动的重大影响在于改变了大坝建设的象征效价。大坝是人类征服自然的象征；它们是最引人注目的国际发展方案之一。20世纪下半叶，大坝成为国家主权的标准。每个国家都想要自己的大坝，多边开发银行希望每个国家都有。2220世纪70和80年代的印尼，大坝被视为国家发展的纪念碑。23反对它们触动了神经。

原页 223, 224

In the hands of protesters, big dams became a symbol of the enmeshment of imperial schemes and national elites, as each disregarded the poor, nature, and the well-being of future generations. Development banks pushed big dams on the nation. Domestic elites, from construction companies to urban power consumers, benefited from their packages. The campaign discredited this combination of foreign design and domestic aggrandizement. Scientists spoke against environmental degradation, democrats spoke of corruption and mismanagement, and villagers spoke of their refusal to be displaced. In this light, foreign and domestic elites appeared self-obsessed and irresponsible. The villagers who refused to be resettled, pictured huddled on rafts and hilltops in the rising water, were compelling icons from central Java, the heartland of Indonesian populism.

原页 223, 224

在抗议者手中，大坝成为帝国计划与国家精英勾结的象征，两者都无视穷人、自然和后代的福祉。开发银行向国家推销大坝。国内精英，从建筑公司到城市电力消费者，从其方案中获益。运动使这种外国设计与国内精英自我扩张的结合失去信誉。科学家发言反对环境退化，民主派谈论腐败和管理不善，村民说出拒绝被迁移。在这种视角下，外国和国内精英显得自恋而不负责任。那些拒绝重新安置的村民，被描绘成蜷缩在上涨水面上的木筏和山顶，成为来自中爪哇——印尼民粹主义腹地——的引人注目的标志。

原页 224

However meager its practical results, this symbolic work—on the critical edge between the national and the transnational—was crucial for contesting national hegemony.

原页 224

无论实际结果多么微薄，这种象征工作——处在国家与跨国层面之间的批判边缘——对挑战国家层面的霸权至关重要。

原页 224

Remaking the Nation in Translation

The global spread of liberalism depends on translation. The terms through which liberalism is to be enacted must be made accessible in new locales. Liberalism is perfectly reproduced only if its language finds universal equivalents. In fact, translation carries cultural genealogies from an original language even as it takes on new genealogies of thought and action from the new language. Concepts are transformed in translation.

原页 224

在翻译中重造民族国家

自由主义的全球传播依赖于翻译。自由主义赖以实施的术语必须在新地方变得可理解。只有当其语言找到普遍对应物，自由主义才被完美复制。事实上，翻译在从新语言获得思想与行动的新谱系时，也把文化谱系从原语言带了过来。概念在翻译中被改变。

原页 224

The environmental movement of the 1980s and 1990s worked hard at translation. Globally influential texts were made available in Indonesian. Campaigns were publicized for the world in English as well as in Indonesian. Much work was also done translating within Indonesia, forming bridges across regional languages and across sectors of society.24 Problems of how to forge dialogues between elite and poor, majority and minority, and urban and rural were pressing; the question of translation stood at the center.

原页 224

20世纪80和90年代的环保运动在翻译上下了很大功夫。有全球影响力的文本被译成印尼文。运动同时用英语和印尼语向世界宣传。印尼内部也做了大量翻译工作，在地区语言和社会各群体之间架起桥梁。24如何在精英与穷人、多数与少数、城市与乡村之间建立对话的问题十分紧迫；翻译问题处在中心。

原页 224

The challenges of translation can be seen in considering the term “indigenous.” The international campaign to save the Amazon rainforest had made the cause of indigenous rights an important tool on the agenda of global environmentalism. In the 1990s, the idea of indigenous rights was spreading. Many Indonesian activists felt that the vitality of this movement would help the cause of displaced and expropriated forest residents in Indonesia. Yet how could this term become a part of an Indonesian movement?

原页 224

考虑“原住民”（indigenous）一词，可以看出翻译的挑战。拯救亚马逊雨林的国际运动使原住民权利事业成为全球环保主义议程上的重要工具。20世纪90年代，原住民权利的观念正在传播。许多印尼活动家感到，这场运动的活力将有助于印尼被迁移和被剥夺的森林居民的事业。然而这个词如何成为印尼运动的一部分？

原页 224, 225

One translation of “indigenous” is pribumi. In most areas, this term did not help activists with their cause. First, this is the term used to exclude Indonesians of Chinese origins from full citizenship; the environmental movement was not willing to endorse this racism.25 Second, Indonesia is not a settler society; the rural victims of resource extraction are mainly of the same stock as urban elites. Except in a few areas, racial categories are irrelevant, but cultural categories are not.26 It is in this context that activists picked masyarakat adat as the translation for “indigenous people.” Adat refers to “custom” and “customary law”; masyarakat adat is customary or “traditional” society. In making the influential International Labor Organization convention on indigenous people available in Indonesian, for example, the translators stress masyarakat adat.27

原页 224, 225

“原住民”的一种译法是 pribumi（土著）。在大多数地区，这个词无助于活动家的事业。第一，这个词被用来把华裔印尼人排除在完整公民身份之外；环保运动不愿支持这种种族主义。25第二，印尼不是移民定居者社会；资源开采的乡村受害者与城市精英大多具有相同的族裔背景。除了少数地区，种族范畴无关紧要，但文化范畴并非如此。26正是在这一背景下，活动家选择 masyarakat adat 作为“原住民”的译法。Adat 指“习俗”与“习惯法”；masyarakat adat 即习惯法社会或“传统”社会。例如，在把有影响力的国际劳工组织原住民公约译成印尼文时，译者强调 masyarakat adat。27

原页 225

The term adat, however, brings its own genealogical baggage. Who has an adat society and who doesn’t? The term can be interpreted as encompassing all Indonesians. It can be limited to those places where formal litigation based on customary law has been supported by colonial and postcolonial authorities. It can be dismissed as a relic, irrelevant even to isolated rural people. It can be used to refer to subjects of colonial treaties—sultanates, chiefdoms. Or it can refer to the subjects of activist campaigns: rural minorities who have suffered from corporate and state resource exploitation.

原页 225

然而，adat 一词带有自身的谱系包袱。谁有习惯法社会，谁没有？这个词可以被解释为涵盖所有印尼人。它可以限于那些基于习惯法的正式诉讼曾受殖民和后殖民当局支持的地方。它可以被贬为遗物，即使对与世隔绝的乡村人也不相关。它可以指殖民条约所涉及的政治实体——苏丹国、酋邦。或者它也可以指活动家运动的对象：遭受公司和政府资源开采之害的乡村少数群体。

原页 225

The reason for this enormous range is the colonial heritage of the term. Dutch colonial authorities used the term to distinguish native customs and laws. For the Dutch, all of native society was ruled by adat except where regulated by European law. The question of what to do with this colonial heritage has not been settled. Modernists want to shelve it as ancient history. Culturalists want to recover it for the nation. Their arguments have been written into a contradictory set of laws. The Basic Agrarian Law of 1960 states that Indonesian law is based on adat, giving the term an important symbolic place. Yet the law does not give adat a practical role. Other laws, such as the Forestry Law of 1975, have extinguished customary rights.28 Still others (e.g., Law 10 of 1992) have reaffirmed them.29 Environmental activists were drawn to the term because of this contradictory legal heritage. The term could remind the public that state and corporate seizures of resources were not the only way the law spoke of property: the dispossessed were represented in those legal texts too—through adat. The term offers more than the pastoralist pleasures of the concept of “tradition” in English. It has facilitated arguments that the state is violating its own rules in refusing to respect forest dwellers’ rights.30

校注4
原页 225

这种巨大范围的原因在于这个词的殖民遗产。荷兰殖民当局用这个词区分原住民习俗与法律。对荷兰人来说，整个原住民社会都由 adat 统治，除非受欧洲法律规范。如何处理这份殖民遗产的问题尚未解决。现代主义者想把它当作古代历史搁置。文化主义者想为民族国家恢复它。他们的论点被写入一套自相矛盾的法律。1960年《基本土地法》规定印尼法律以 adat 为基础，赋予该词重要的象征位置。然而法律并未赋予 adat 实际作用。其他法律，如1975年《森林法》，则取消了习惯权利。28还有一些法律（如1992年第10号法）重申了这些权利。29环保活动家被这个词吸引，正是因为这种矛盾的法律遗产。这个词可以提醒公众，国家和公司夺取资源并非法律谈论财产的唯一方式：被剥夺者在那些法律文本中也有代表——通过 adat。这个词提供的，不只是英语“传统”概念那种田园诗般的愉悦。它促进了这样的论证：国家在拒绝尊重森林居民权利时，违反了自己的规则。30

校注4
原页 225, 226

The rhetoric of rights for masyarakat adat engendered fierce debate among activists. Some derided it as romantis, “romantic,” and claimed that all traditions today are bogus. Some saw it as a feudal heritage that should be replaced by modern law. Others found it the most useful conceptual tool in their advocacy for forest dwellers, allowing them to explain why New Order systems of resource exploitation were wrong. Some spoke for migrants, arguing against the privileging of aboriginal inhabitants. Others showed the loss to conservation and human rights that followed from uprooting indigenous livelihoods. Most important, through conferences, documents, legal cases, and training sessions, the term forged a growing network linking embattled rural people.

原页 225, 226

为 masyarakat adat 争取权利的修辞在活动家中引发激烈辩论。一些人讥讽它“浪漫”（romantis），声称今天的一切传统都是伪造的。一些人视之为封建遗产，应以现代法取代。另一些人发现它是倡导森林居民时最有用的概念工具，使他们能够解释新秩序的资源开采制度为何错误。一些人为移民发声，反对给予原居住民特权。另一些人则指出，连根拔起原住民生计会给保护和人权带来损失。最重要的是，通过会议、文件、法律案件和培训，这个词锻造了一个不断扩大的网络，把陷入困境的乡村人民连接起来。

原页 226

This network of adat advocacy was particularly effective for those marginalized rural people who had not been recognized as having any rights at all—through adat or otherwise. These newly recognized masyarakat adat could now imagine themselves as more than “isolated tribes,” the untutored clods of state propaganda; their difference made them, if anything, better citizens.31 For these new citizens of adat, tradition formed a critical lens through which to de-naturalize coercive development and demand social justice.

原页 226

这种 adat 倡导网络，对那些完全未被承认拥有任何权利——无论通过 adat 还是其他方式——的边缘化乡村人民尤其有效。这些新获承认的 masyarakat adat 现在可以把自己想象为不只是“与世隔绝的部落”，即国家宣传中没有教养的土包子；如果说有什么的话，他们的差异使他们成为更好的公民。31对这些 adat 的新公民来说，传统形成了一个批判透镜，通过它可以把强制发展去自然化，并要求社会正义。

原页 226

This critique, indeed, stretched into the immediate post-New Order period. In 1999, the indigenous advocacy network gelled in an archipelagowide alliance, the Aliansi Masyarakat Adat Nusantara (AMAN). The choice of the term nusantara, “archipelago,” to unite the assembled representatives of masyarakat adat was carefully planned. The nation, indigenous activists argued, had discredited itself by refusing to recognize their rights; they were unwilling to use the word nasional. Yet they wanted a nationwide gathering to contest state policies and plan alternatives in coalition. Nusantara was an elegant way to call up and criticize the nation simultaneously, a gesture at the heart of utopian critique.32

原页 226

这种批评确实延伸到新秩序之后的时期。1999年，原住民倡导网络凝结成一个全群岛联盟——群岛习惯法社群联盟（Aliansi Masyarakat Adat Nusantara，AMAN）。选择 nusantara（“群岛”）一词来团结与会 masyarakat adat 代表是精心策划的。原住民活动家论证说，国家因拒绝承认他们的权利而自毁信誉；他们不愿使用 nasional（国家的／全国的）一词。然而他们想要一场全国性集会，以联盟形式挑战国家政策并规划替代方案。Nusantara 是一种同时召唤和批评国家的优雅方式，是乌托邦批评核心的姿态。32

原页 226

At the same time, the alliance was charged with the contradictions of its invocation through adat.33 What relations should hold between those who claimed adat through colonial treaties versus those who had advocacy causes? Opposition to the state would not hold together populist politics much longer. Did these dispersed groups have anything else in common? Would they find a negotiating point with modernists, Muslim and secular, who refused adat-based politics? Post-New Order problems emerged: political disorientation, ethnic and religious conflict, and competition among alternative future visions. The endless horizon of the New Order no longer defined the political landscape.

原页 226

与此同时，这个联盟也充满其通过 adat 发出的召唤所包含的矛盾。33通过殖民条约主张 adat 的人与有倡导事业的人之间应保持何种关系？反对国家的立场不会在更长时间里维系民粹主义政治。这些分散的群体还有别的共同点吗？他们会与现代主义者——拒绝以 adat 为基础的政治的穆斯林和世俗主义者——找到协商的交汇点吗？新秩序后的问题出现了：政治迷失、族群与宗教冲突，以及另类未来愿景之间的竞争。新秩序无尽的地平线不再界定政治地景。

原页 226

The Change

原页 226

变革

原页 226, 227

In May 1998, President Suharto was forced to step down, handing the government to his associate Habibie and opening the way for general elections. The beginning of the end had come earlier, in the 1997 financial crisis and the subsequent ultimatums of the International Monetary Fund, which threatened not only to open up the crony system but also to withdraw popular subsidies for rice and oil. The New Order had lost its promises of wealth—and its international backing. Without these, domestic unrest soared. Students mobilized. Demonstrations and riots filled city streets. The New Order fell.

原页 226, 227

1998年5月，苏哈托总统被迫下台，把政府交给同僚哈比比，并为大选开辟道路。终结的开端更早到来，即1997年金融危机以及随后国际货币基金组织的最后通牒，后者不仅威胁要打破裙带体系的封闭性，还要取消大米和石油的民众补贴。新秩序失去了财富承诺——也失去了国际支持。失去这些之后，国内动荡飙升。学生动员起来。示威和骚乱充斥城市街道。新秩序倒台。

原页 227

Politics opened up. Taxi drivers speculated about what they would do as president. Repressed ideologies emerged with force. Radical Islam spread. Bookstores filled with Marxist texts. Political posturing and debate spread to the countryside, so long in silence. Community groups mounted protests. Some took over logging and mining base camps and destroyed equipment. Meanwhile, the army and gangsters spread violence. Ethnic and religious conflicts flared up. In 2000, resource policy decentralization transferred resource struggles, bribes, and arrangements to the lowest levels of the state bureaucracy. Instead of advocating for community groups, national environmentalists found themselves in a position as mediators between destructive villagers and enraged companies. Activists in Jakarta struggled to keep up with the changing situation. Sometimes they tried to make policy; sometimes they formed an opposition. Long retreats became necessary to sort things out. In the countryside, however, activism gained a new bravery and initiative. Jakarta was no longer the center of movement possibilities. In the provinces, a new dynamic of utopianism superceded national critique.

原页 227

政治开放了。出租车司机猜测自己当总统会做什么。被压抑的意识形态强力浮现。激进伊斯兰传播。书店摆满马克思主义文本。政治姿态和辩论蔓延到长期沉默的乡村。社群团体发起抗议。一些人占领伐木和采矿营地，毁坏设备。与此同时，军队和黑帮散播暴力。族群和宗教冲突爆发。2000年，资源政策分权把资源争夺、贿赂和安排转移到国家官僚机构的最低层级。全国环保主义者不是为社群团体倡导，而是发现自己处在破坏性村民和愤怒公司之间的调解人位置。雅加达的活动家努力跟上变化的形势。有时他们试图制定政策；有时他们形成反对派。为了理清事情，长时间的闭门研讨成为必要。然而在乡村，行动主义获得了新的勇气和主动性。雅加达不再是运动可能性的中心。在各省，乌托邦主义的新动态取代了国家层面的批判。

原页 227

Tracking Traveling Stories

原页 227

追踪旅行的故事

原页 227

After 1998, politics moved to the countryside. Decentralization was not just a financial plan; oppositional politics, no longer centered in Jakarta, devolved to ethnic, religious, and regional struggles. Regional causes found their own transnational resources. Now that activists could take the nation apart, their biggest problem was the very caution that shaped New Order activism. How could something stronger be stirred up?

原页 227

1998年后，政治转移到乡村。分权不只是财政计划；反对政治不再以雅加达为中心，而是下放到族群、宗教和地区斗争。地区事业找到了自己的跨国资源。既然活动家可以把国家拆解，他们最大的问题正是塑造新秩序行动主义的谨慎。如何激起更强大的东西？

原页 227

Activist stories in the provinces grew braver and wilder. My own storytelling responds: Where I have shadowed national objectives in solidarity with movement efforts, I open up to something more freewheeling. My questions move out from the anchor of the nation; hit-and-miss opportunities of mobility and mobilization are suddenly more relevant. How does political agency grow in times of flux?

原页 227

各省的活动家故事变得更勇敢、更狂野。我自己的叙事作出回应：此前，我为声援运动的努力而紧随国家目标展开叙述；现在，我转向更自由奔放的叙述。我的问题从国家这一锚点向外移动；流动性与动员的试错机会突然更具相关性。政治能动性在流动时期如何成长？

原页 227, 228

In the next sections, I show how activism moves in “charismatic packages,” allegorical modules that speak to the possibilities of making a cause heard. These packages feature images, songs, morals, organizational plans, or stories. They introduce us to heroes and villains; they show us how an unrepresented group can become a political force. Like all socially effective allegories, activist packages are formed in a political and cultural location that gives their stories meaning and makes them work as social interventions. This location need not be a single place; it may be a widespread political culture, or the meeting point between two or more political cultures. When an activist package is brought to a new location, it must enter new fields of meaning and of social action to make a difference in its new home. The effect of a new allegory is most striking when it inspires unexpected social collaborations, which realign the social field. We might speak of “happy collaborations”—not joyful but felicitous; in coming together, they make a difference in what counts as politics.

原页 227, 228

在接下来的几节中，我展示行动主义如何在“富有感召力的包裹”中移动，这些寓言模块诉说着让一项事业被听见的可能性。这些包裹包含图像、歌曲、道德、组织计划或故事。它们向我们介绍英雄和反派；它们展示一个未被代表的群体如何成为政治力量。像所有社会有效的寓言一样，行动主义包裹形成于一个政治与文化位置，这位置赋予其故事意义，使它们作为社会干预发挥作用。这个位置不必是单一地点；它可能是一种广泛传播的政治文化，或是两种或多种政治文化之间的交汇点。当行动主义包裹被带到新地点，它必须进入新的意义场域和社会行动场域，才能在新家发挥作用。新寓言的影响最显著之时，是它激发出意外的社会合作，从而重新排列社会场域。我们或许可以谈论“幸运的合作”——不是欢乐，而是相宜；在走到一起时，它们改变了何谓政治。

原页 228

This model of analysis is indebted to the everyday practices of activists in transnational NGO politics, who spend much of their time in workshops trading stories of success and failure. Yet it is a difficult practice for scholars, who are properly anxious about learning enough about far-flung sites to tell globetrotting right. One can appreciate this kind of activism, however, only by taking the risk of stretching beyond one’s scholarly base. Sometimes the point for activists is to borrow allegories unmoored from their home contexts and not yet bent to the niceties of local negotiation; these are allegories that can be tapped for unpopular and minority causes. To see the potential as well as the limitations of such stories, one must consider how they draw people here and there to retell them.

原页 228

这种分析模型得益于跨国非政府组织政治中活动家的日常实践，他们花大量时间在工作坊里交换成功与失败的故事。然而这对学者是一种困难的实践，学者理应担心要了解足够多关于遥远地点的知识，才能正确地讲述环球旅行。然而，只有承担超越自身学术基地的风险，才能欣赏这类行动主义。对活动家来说，要点有时是借用脱离其家乡语境、尚未被地方协商的精细要求所弯曲的寓言；这些寓言可以为不受欢迎的事业和少数群体的事业所用。要看到这类故事的潜力与局限，必须考虑它们如何吸引此处与彼处的人们去重述它们。

原页 228, 229

Let me begin by taking you with me on a trip to the Meratus Mountains with three activists from the Lembaga Pemberdayaan Masyarakat Adat Borneo Selatan (LPMA), the Empowerment Institute for Indigenous People of South Borneo. The activists are mainly urban educated Muslims, from the Banjar regional majority, advocating for non-Muslim forest dwellers. This is a challenging assignment. It is the summer of 2000. The LPMA has rented a house in the provincial capital, Banjarmasin, where activists work and talk all day and sometimes through the night. There are media events to host, conferences to plan, reports and budgets to write, grants to pursue, position papers to hammer out—and, after hours, existential and political questions about what makes all this worthwhile. The most active members have graduated from college and not yet moved to other forms of employment, so they have time—plus impressive amounts of imagination, intensity, and stamina. When I arrive at the office early in the morning for our trip, I find that my traveling companions—two young women and one young man—have been up most of the night, but still they have more energy than I can imagine, and we bounce off into the day. The public van in which we will travel refuses to leave until every seat is taken, and we sit packed, motionless, and sweating for several hours before, at last, we can feel the wind off the road. At some point, tired of chatter with strangers, I pretend to be asleep, but my activist friends still patiently explain to all the other passengers why nice, middle-class, young Muslims like themselves might expose themselves to danger and horror among the impious savages of the Meratus jungles. It is especially hard for the women, who must maintain an air of respectability while admitting that they will be beyond supervision. We will be spending most of the week in rough surroundings with no privacy. Perhaps they are thinking of this too when they tease each other playfully about potential boyfriends and girlfriends; I gather that their friendship is platonic. Besides, they are experienced travelers; being an activist involves constant travel.

原页 228, 229

让我先带你们与三位来自南婆罗洲习惯法社群赋权机构（Lembaga Pemberdayaan Masyarakat Adat Borneo Selatan，LPMA）的活动家一起去梅拉图斯山脉。这些活动家主要是受过城市教育的穆斯林，来自班贾尔地区多数族群，为非穆斯林的森林居民争取权益。这是一项艰巨任务。那是2000年夏天。LPMA 在省会班贾尔马辛租了一所房子，活动家们整天在那里工作和交谈，有时通宵达旦。要举办媒体活动、规划会议、撰写报告和预算、申请资助、敲定立场文件——还在下班后讨论存在主义和政治问题：这一切究竟为何值得。最活跃的成员已大学毕业，尚未转向其他形式就业，所以有时间——还有令人印象深刻的想象力、投入程度和耐力。清早我到办公室准备出发时，发现我的旅伴——两位年轻女性和一位年轻男性——大半宿没睡，但他们的精力仍超乎我的想象，我们一路颠簸进入新的一天。我们要乘坐的公共小巴要等每个座位都坐满才肯出发，我们挤在一起，一动不动，汗流浃背地坐了好几个小时，终于才感觉到路上的风。某个时候，我厌倦了与陌生人闲聊，假装睡着，但我的活动家朋友仍在耐心地向所有其他乘客解释，为什么像他们这样善良的中产阶级年轻穆斯林，会让自己在梅拉图斯丛林不敬神的野蛮人中面对危险与恐怖。女性尤其艰难，她们必须保持体面的神态，同时承认自己将不受监督。我们将在没有隐私的粗陋环境中度过一周的大部分时间。也许他们拿可能交往的男女朋友互相打趣时，也想到了这一点；我猜他们之间是纯粹的友谊。再说，他们是经验丰富的旅行者；做活动家就意味着不断旅行。

原页 229

After half a day in the van, we transfer to motorcycle taxis to navigate the steep and muddy hillside tracks. As evening falls, we arrive in the Meratus village of Niwan. I haven’t been there for several years, and I am pleased that people remember me, although my best friends have died or moved elsewhere. Yet I press away other invitations to stick with the activists, who have moved their things into the house of one of their village allies. They are worried: they have found themselves in a dilemma. Their task here is to convene a meeting about the map-making exercise that has become an important project of the LPMA. They have trained Meratus community groups to make maps of their village territories using Global Positioning System equipment. In these times of change, it seems at least possible that these maps might influence government policy to prevent corporate theft. Yet, not surprisingly, they have run into a problem with boundaries; adjacent villages claim overlapping territorial reaches. This meeting was to have clarified the boundary between Niwan and a neighboring village. I am not at all shocked when it turns out that none of the key leaders from either village have made themselves available for the meeting; they are all reported to be sick or away on a pressing errand.

原页 229

在面包车里待了半天后，我们换乘摩托车出租车，穿行陡峭泥泞的山坡小径。傍晚时分，我们抵达梅拉图斯村庄尼万。我已好几年没去过那里，我很高兴人们还记得我，尽管我最好的朋友已经去世或搬走。但我推掉了其他邀请，坚持跟着活动家们，他们已经把东西搬进一位村中盟友的家。他们很担心：他们发现自己陷入两难。他们在这里的任务是召集一次关于制图行动的会议，这已成为 LPMA 的重要项目。他们培训了梅拉图斯社群团体使用全球定位系统设备绘制村领地地图。在这个变化的时代，这些地图至少有可能影响政府政策，阻止公司盗窃。然而不出所料，他们遇到了边界问题；相邻村庄主张重叠的领土范围。这次会议本应澄清尼万与一个邻村之间的边界。当结果发现两村的关键领袖都没有空参加会议——据报都病了或出门办紧急事务——我一点也不震惊。

原页 229, 230

Still, the LPMA activists make the best of their time. They hand out the colorful posters they have designed for the anti-Kodeco campaign. They catch up with local gossip. After dinner, we convene an informal meeting. Some of my friends have come; others are friends of the LPMA team. We talk about the bad prices of rubber, the major local cash crop. The villagers complain that they must take whatever price comes their way. The activists have a plan: If all the villagers hoard their rubber, they can negotiate for higher prices. Their audience is not convinced. How can individuals coordinate, when everyone wants the money immediately? We go back and forth, with the activists arguing that collective action will pay off, and their Meratus interlocutors remaining skeptical. It is then that one of my activist companions launches into a story.

“There was a man named Chico,” she says, “and he brought together the rubber tappers to oppose the felling of the rainforest.” She is speaking of Chico Mendes, the legendary leader of the Brazilian rubber tappers movement who was murdered in 1988. We had moved from rubber prices to community rights to the forest—and the logging controversy. But even here, we all knew that there was Meratus skepticism about the power of community-based political action. Her story of Chico Mendes was an inspirational one about the possibility of effective mobilization.

原页 229, 230

尽管如此，LPMA 活动家还是充分利用时间。他们分发为反 Kodeco 运动设计的彩色海报。他们打听当地近来的闲话。晚饭后，我们召开一次非正式会议。我的一些朋友来了；另一些是 LPMA 团队的朋友。我们谈论橡胶——当地主要经济作物——的糟糕价格。村民抱怨只能接受别人给的价格。活动家有一个计划：如果所有村民都囤积橡胶，他们就可以谈判更高的价格。听众并不信服。每个人都想马上拿到钱，个人怎么能协调？我们来来回回，活动家论证集体行动会有回报，他们的梅拉图斯对话者仍然怀疑。就在这时，我的一位活动家同伴开始讲故事。

“有一个叫奇科的人，”她说，“他把橡胶采集者团结起来，反对砍伐雨林。”她说的是奇科·门德斯，巴西橡胶采集者运动的传奇领袖，1988年被谋杀。我们从橡胶价格谈到了社群对森林的权利——以及伐木争议。但即使在这里，我们都知道梅拉图斯人对以社群为基础的政治行动的力量存有怀疑。她讲的奇科·门德斯故事是一个鼓舞人心的故事，讲述有效动员的可能性。

原页 230

I jump in, eager to stress this point. “The amazing thing about Chico was that he was successful,” I say, awkwardly attempting to translate the idea of “extractive reserves.” Perhaps because I am so engaged in my point, what happened next makes my head spin. The woman telling the story drives the message home. “When they came to cut down the forest,” she says, “the women came out and hugged the trees.” She reaches her arms out, miming the hugging of trees, and the other woman activist joins her, showing people how the women hugged the trees.

原页 230

我插话，急于强调这一点。“奇科了不起的地方在于他成功了，”我说，笨拙地试图翻译“林产品采集保护区”的概念。也许因为我太投入自己的观点，接下来发生的事让我头晕目眩。讲故事的女人把信息讲透。“当他们来砍森林时，”她说，“女人们出来抱住树。”她伸出双臂，模仿抱树的动作，另一位女活动家也加入她，向人们展示女人们如何抱树。

原页 230

I believe we have moved from Chico to Chipko, from the rubber tappers of the Amazon to the foothills of the Himalayas where women came out to protect the forest by hugging the trees, thus the name Chipko, hugging.34 It is an easy enough slippage. Both are famous examples of grassroots organizing for forest protection. Both are models for environmental NGOs around the world. But I can’t help but smile—and pause. How have these stories arrived there? Why are international stories important to these activists? It is then that I first consider the possibility of taking apart this story, in telling more stories that precede it and make it possible. This may at least offer a sense of why two young activist women might feel empowered not only to flaunt convention in their personal behavior but also to inspire others with a sense of political direction.

原页 230

我相信我们已经从奇科滑到了契普科，从亚马逊的橡胶采集者滑到了喜马拉雅山麓，那里的女人出来抱树保护森林，因而得名契普科（Chipko），意为“拥抱”。34这是一个很容易的滑移。两者都是基层森林保护组织的著名例子。两者都是世界各地环保非政府组织的榜样。但我忍不住微笑——并停顿。这些故事是如何到达那里的？为什么国际故事对这些活动家重要？就在这时，我第一次考虑拆解这个故事的可能性，讲述更多先于它并使之可能的故事。这至少可以让人理解，为什么两位年轻女活动家会感到有力量，不仅可以在个人行为上蔑视常规，还能以政治方向感激励他人。

原页 230

In the next sections, I follow the activist allegory of Chico Mendes, with an occasional nod to Chipko. Such stories travel because they tell of conditions of solidarity, because they follow established channels of mediation, and because they augment budding conversations about the possibilities of political agency. These elements remind us that political modules can only make politics through friction. Activists are drawn to these stories about local community and global solidarity, but they cannot just replicate them. To track traveling stories is to show their transformations.

原页 230

在接下来的几节中，我追随奇科·门德斯的行动主义寓言，偶尔也提一下契普科。这类故事之所以旅行，是因为它们讲述团结的状况，遵循既定的中介渠道，并拓展正在萌芽的关于政治能动性可能性的对话。这些要素提醒我们，政治模块只能通过摩擦制造政治。活动家被这些关于地方社群与全球团结的故事吸引，但他们不能只复制它们。追踪旅行的故事，就是展示它们的转变。

原页 230

I begin by tracing the Chico Mendes story as it moved from Brazil to North America to Malaysia, and from there to Indonesia. Indonesians rejected this package in the early 1990s, only to accept it at the end of the decade. To understand why it is necessary to consider how the allegorical module was formulated—and transformed—in the specific trajectory of its movements. A Brazil-North America collaboration formed its elements, but these were repackaged in Malaysia in ways that made the package anathema to Indonesians—until after 1998.

原页 230

我先追踪奇科·门德斯的故事，从巴西到北美再到马来西亚，然后到印尼。印尼人在20世纪90年代初拒绝了这一包裹，直到90年代末才接受。要理解原因，必须考虑寓言模块在其运动的具体轨迹中是如何形成——并转变——的。巴西—北美合作形成了它的要素，但这些要素在马来西亚被重新包装，使这个包裹对印尼人成为可憎之物——直到1998年之后。

原页 231

The Uses of Alliance

原页 231

联盟的用处

原页 231

How do allegorical packages form models for solidarity?

原页 231

寓言包裹如何形成团结的模型？

原页 231

Viewed from very far away, the most important thing about Chico Mendes’s fight against Amazon deforestation was the fact that it was not just a grassroots struggle, but also something larger—something that came to be referred to as global environmentalism. International protest against Mendes’s assassination in 1988 sparked an outpouring of concern about the rainforest that leapt from one place to another; in hindsight, it was the high point of global rainforest mobilization. But what did “global” mean here? Most impressively, it referred to the possibility of a movement that could involve poor rural Brazilians, Brazilian elites, and northern advocates in a common cause.35

原页 231

从很远的地方看，奇科·门德斯反对亚马逊森林砍伐的斗争最重要之处在于，它不只是一场基层斗争，还是一项更大的事物——一项后来被称为全球环保主义的事物。1988年门德斯被暗杀后，国际抗议引发了对雨林的关切洪流，从一个地方跳到另一个地方；事后看来，那是全球雨林动员的高峰。但这里的“全球”意味着什么？最令人印象深刻的是，它指一场运动有可能把贫穷的巴西乡村人、巴西精英和北方倡导者纳入共同事业。35

原页 231

This was no easy achievement. Earlier mobilizations to save the Amazon rainforest had received a cold welcome in Brazil. At the height of the success of Brazilian development, conservationists and indigenous rights advocates were seen as inspired by meddling foreigners.36 The military government called them subversives. The opening of the Amazon was the road to national development (Keck 1995a).

原页 231

这并非轻易成就。早先拯救亚马逊雨林的动员在巴西受到冷遇。在巴西发展成功的顶峰时期，保护主义者和原住民权利倡导者被视为受外国干预者煽动。36军政府称他们为颠覆分子。开放亚马逊是通往国家发展的道路（Keck 1995a）。

原页 231

Chico Mendes and the rubber tappers came to rainforest politics from a different direction. Mendes entered politics through the trade union movement. In 1979, he joined the Workers’ Party, which united church groups, intellectuals, and workers to form a progressive opposition to military government. The early actions of the rubber tappers were union actions, organized in the idioms of Brazilian workers’ politics (Keck 1995b). The rubber tappers only joined with conservationists and indigenous advocates in the mid-1980s.

校注6
原页 231

奇科·门德斯和橡胶采集者从另一个方向进入雨林政治。门德斯通过工会运动进入政治。1979年，他加入劳工党，该党联合教会团体、知识分子和工人，形成对军政府的进步反对派。橡胶采集者的早期行动是工会行动，以巴西工人政治的语汇组织（Keck 1995b）。橡胶采集者直到20世纪80年代中期才与保护主义者和原住民倡导者联合。

校注6
原页 231, 232

It was this happy collaboration, however, that opened the door for a new local/global politics, both Brazilian and transnational, combining and conflating the poetics and demands of social justice, the environment, and indigenous cultural survival. A new way of imagining what is politically possible formed within the affiliation of social groups. Workers’ politics made possible a national Brazilian involvement, suddenly the movement to save the Amazon could be portrayed as a national cause. Transnational support empowered Brazilian voices. Transnational support in this case was mainly North American; this was explicitly a north-south collaboration. Mendes was an important architect of this collaboration: His trips to the United States to seek environmentalist allies and to influence policy makers were key to making protection of the Amazon an issue imagined as “global.” Meanwhile, his call for extractive reserves, that is forests protected for rubber, brazil nuts, and other economic products, articulated a meeting point for conservation and economic justice (Mendes 1989).

The happy collaboration did not last long; and it is still debated how much good it has done rubber tappers. However, the charisma of this activist package was enormous, and it inspired rainforest mobilizations elsewhere. It also dragged along its own deeply located culture and politics, which were key in spreading the idea that activism could be both global and grassroots. The concept of “forest people,” not just indigenous but rural workers, deexoticized the rainforest, making it possible to argue that social justice rather than elite privilege was at stake. The extractive reserves model made it possible to think that preservation and profit could go together, opening an era of experimentation for environmental entrepreneurship. Finally, negotiations between Brazilian and North American activists gave new weight to the global claims of conservationists. The southern connection gave northerners a claim of collaborative, rather than merely imperial, globality; this was a globality that worked, the allegory said, to empower the grass roots.

原页 231, 232

然而正是这种幸运的合作，为一种新的地方/全球政治打开了大门，既是巴西的也是跨国的，结合并融合了社会正义、环境和原住民文化生存的诗学与诉求。一种想象政治可能性的新方式在社会群体的联合中形成。工人政治使巴西的全国参与成为可能，突然之间，拯救亚马逊的运动可以被描绘为一项国家事业。跨国支持赋予巴西声音力量。这里的跨国支持主要是北美的；这明确是一场南北合作。门德斯是这种合作的重要建筑师：他前往美国寻求环保主义者盟友并影响政策制定者，这是使亚马逊保护被想象为“全球”议题的关键。与此同时，他关于林产品采集保护区——即为橡胶、巴西坚果和其他经济产品而保护的森林——的呼吁，阐述了保护与经济正义的汇合点（Mendes 1989）。

这场幸运的合作没有持续多久；它对橡胶采集者究竟有多大益处，至今仍有争议。然而，这个行动主义包裹的感召力巨大，它激发了别处的雨林动员。它还拖带着自身深植的文化和政治，这些在传播“行动主义可以既是全球的又是基层的”这一观念时至关重要。“森林人民”的概念——不只是原住民，还包括乡村工人——使雨林去异域化，使人们可以论证攸关的是社会正义而非精英特权。林产品采集保护区模式使人们可以认为保护与利润可以并存，开启了环境创业的实验时代。最后，巴西与北美活动家之间的谈判赋予保护主义者的全球主张新的分量。南方联系让北方人获得一种合作而非纯粹帝国的全球性主张；这个寓言说，这种全球性致力于赋权基层。

原页 232

Northern environmentalists took the Chico Mendes story as a mandate for their intervention wherever rainforests were threatened. The allegory for them was the story of “global” nature lovers helping vulnerable forest people. They underplayed the role of national collaborations, such as the Brazil—United States ties made possible by Mendes’s union politics. This problem was particularly striking in the next “global” rainforest campaign: the movement to save the forests of Sarawak, Malaysia, and to empower the Penan hunter-gatherers who lived there. The Malaysian campaign reformulated the Chico Mendes story, making a new traveling package that was unattractive for Indonesian environmentalists.37

原页 232

北方环保主义者把奇科·门德斯的故事当作在雨林受威胁之处进行干预的授权。对他们来说，寓言是“全球”自然爱好者帮助脆弱森林人民的故事。他们淡化国家合作的作用，例如门德斯的工会政治促成的巴西—美国联系。这个问题在下一场“全球”雨林运动中尤为突出：拯救马来西亚沙捞越森林并赋权居住在那里的本南狩猎采集者的运动。马来西亚运动重新表述了奇科·门德斯的故事，制造了一个对印尼环保主义者没有吸引力的新旅行包裹。37

原页 232, 233

Malaysia had a strong environmental movement by the 1980s. But this was economic miracle time in Southeast Asia. Economic strength gave the Mahathir regime the authority to keep all opposition very quiet. In 1987, opposition leaders were rounded up and imprisoned. Still, groups such as Sahabat Alam Malaysia, SAM, were lively participants in publicizing the need for forest and forest people’s protection.38

In 1987, a group of Penan blockaded timber roads to protest logging, and this caught the attention of northern environmentalists.39 A transnational campaign ensued: Following the model set in the Amazon, northerners imagined themselves as transnational support for a local cause. Yet everything went differently in Malaysia. The transnational campaign too often ignored SAM. The Penan were nostalgic for colonial rule and asked white environmentalists to protect them (Brosius 2003a). The key interlocutor was not a Malaysian national progressive but rather a Swiss artist named Bruno Manser, who had gone into the forests and made the Penan cause his own (Manser 1996). Manser was an articulate and passionate spokesperson, but he could not make the cause a Malaysian one. Instead, he was an illegal alien, a romantic European without ties to national elites. When he disappeared in 2001, probably murdered, no Malaysians raised a public cry.

校注7
原页 232, 233

到20世纪80年代，马来西亚已有强大的环保运动。但那是东南亚的经济奇迹时期。经济实力赋予马哈蒂尔政权让所有反对派保持沉默的权威。1987年，反对派领袖被围捕入狱。尽管如此，马来西亚自然之友（Sahabat Alam Malaysia，SAM）等团体仍是宣传森林和森林人民保护需求的活跃参与者。38

1987年，一群本南人封锁运材道路，抗议伐木，这引起北方环保主义者的注意。39随后展开一场跨国运动：遵循亚马逊树立的模式，北方人把自己想象为对地方事业的跨国支持。然而在马来西亚，一切都不同。跨国运动常常忽视 SAM。本南人怀念殖民统治，并请求白人环保主义者保护他们（Brosius 2003a）。关键对话者不是马来西亚本国的进步人士，而是一位名叫布鲁诺·曼瑟的瑞士艺术家，他深入森林，把本南人的事业变成自己的事业（Manser 1996）。曼瑟是一位口齿清楚、充满激情的发言人，但他无法让这项事业成为马来西亚的事业。相反，他是一个非法居留的外国人，一个与国家精英没有联系的浪漫欧洲人。2001年他失踪，可能被谋杀，没有马来西亚人公开发声。

校注7
原页 233

Instead, the cry of vulnerability came from the Malaysian government. This is eco-imperialism, said Prime Minister Mahathir: the imposition of a northern cause on a southern people. They are trying to deny forest people the right to development; they want to keep them in a zoo (Brosius 1999b). Malaysian progressives, disgruntled by the tactics of northern environmentalists, joined Mahathir, making this repackaging particularly strong. With this rallying cry, Malaysia led pro-development southern regimes at the United Nations’ 1992 environmental summit in Rio, as Brazil had in 1972 in Stockholm. The forests would be felled for national sovereignty and social justice. The Chico Mendes story, in translation, had changed. A new allegory was created, and it, too, was traveling.

原页 233

相反，声称自身处境脆弱的呼声来自马来西亚政府。“这是生态帝国主义，”马哈蒂尔总理说：把北方事业强加给南方人民。他们试图剥夺森林人民的发展权；他们想把他们关在动物园里（Brosius 1999b）。马来西亚进步人士对北方环保主义者的策略不满，加入马哈蒂尔，使这种重新包装尤为有力。凭借这一战斗口号，马来西亚在1992年联合国里约环境峰会上领导支持发展的南方政权，正如巴西1972年在斯德哥尔摩所做的那样。森林将为国家主权和社会正义而被砍伐。奇科·门德斯的故事在翻译中已经改变。一个新的寓言被创造出来，它也在旅行。

原页 233

In this context Indonesian national environmentalists of the 1990s wanted nothing to do with the Chico Mendes story and its allegorical implications. Indonesians had carefully built a national environmental movement under a repressive regime. They had worked with sympathetic bureaucrats and appealed to engineers as well as social idealists. This was not a period to get involved with irresponsible northerners. The allegory would not stimulate a national social intervention. No happy collaboration was in sight.

原页 233

在这种背景下，20世纪90年代的印尼全国环保主义者不想与奇科·门德斯的故事及其寓言含义有任何关系。印尼人在一个压制性政权下精心建设了一场全国环保运动。他们与同情他们的官僚合作，既诉诸工程师，也诉诸社会理想主义者。这不是卷入不负责任的北方人的时候。这个寓言不会激发全国性的社会干预。看不到幸运的合作。

原页 233

When one northern activist tried to mount a transnational campaign to protect a group of Indonesian Dayaks in the mid-1990s, echoing Chico Mendes as well as Bruno Manser, environmental leaders in Jakarta sprang into action to stop it. Indonesian activists agreed that local livelihoods were being destroyed. But they did not want a repetition of the Sarawak campaign, with its local/global allegories. They contacted their U.S. and European supporters to stop the campaign before it could develop. Instead, they worked domestically, negotiating across government bureaucracies to advocate for the group. The disasters of the Sarawak campaign ushered in a period of careful nationalism on the part of Indonesian activists. They were willing to accept northern funds, but it was important to keep policy and politics as a domestic matter.

原页 233

20世纪90年代中期，当一位北方活动家试图发起一场跨国运动，保护一群印尼达雅克人，呼应奇科·门德斯和布鲁诺·曼瑟时，雅加达的环保领袖立即行动阻止。印尼活动家同意当地生计正被破坏。但他们不想重演沙捞越运动及其地方/全球寓言。他们联系美国和欧洲的支持者，在运动发展起来之前阻止它。相反，他们在国内工作，跨政府官僚机构谈判，为这群人倡导。沙捞越运动的灾难为印尼活动家带来了一个谨慎民族主义的时期。他们愿意接受北方资金，但重要的是把政策和政治保持为国内事务。

原页 233

Everything changed in 1998 when the Suharto regime fell. Political democracy seemed possible; chaos moved through the countryside. LPMA activists were in a hurry; everything might be changed if they worked quickly, before the time of change ended. What they needed was a disciplined grassroots activism that knew how to build alliances rather than burn down camps. For this the Chico Mendes story spoke eloquently, evoking the possibility of local/global alliances that empowered communities and made possible both conservation and justice.

原页 233

1998年苏哈托政权倒台后，一切都变了。政治民主似乎可能；混乱席卷乡村。LPMA 活动家很匆忙；如果他们在变革时期结束前快速工作，一切都可能改变。他们需要的是一种有纪律的基层行动主义，懂得如何建立联盟而不是烧毁营地。为此，奇科·门德斯的故事雄辩地发言，唤起地方/全球联盟的可能性，这种联盟赋权社群，并使保护与正义同时成为可能。

原页 233, 234

Chico Mendes’s story established several contradictory models of solidarity, from union politics to north-south collaboration to eco-imperialism. As the story moved from place to place, its allegorical possibilities grew. Its trajectory followed power-laden circuits and squeezed into conjunctural openings. My next section turns to these.

原页 233, 234

奇科·门德斯的故事确立了几种相互矛盾的团结模式，从工会政治到南北合作再到生态帝国主义。随着故事从一个地方移动到另一个地方，它的寓言可能性不断增长。它的轨迹遵循充满权力的环路，并挤入时机性的开口。我下一节转向这些。

原页 234

Mediating Circumstances

A distinctive feature of the travels of the Chico Mendes story was its travel through the north. It is the story northern environmentalists made of Mendes that became significant elsewhere. No Brazilian union leaders came to organize rubber tappers in Malaysia; northern environmentalists—with their package-spreading money, media, and passports—were almost entirely responsible for making the story speak to Southeast Asians. Some translators have privileged access to making and distributing packages.

原页 234

中介境况

奇科·门德斯故事流传的一个显著特征，是它经由北方的旅行。北方环保主义者制造的关于门德斯的故事，才是在别处变得重要的故事。没有巴西工会领袖前来马来西亚组织橡胶采集者；北方环保主义者——带着他们传播包裹的资金、媒体和护照——几乎完全负责让这个故事对东南亚人说话。一些翻译者拥有制造和分发包裹的特权渠道。

原页 234

Activist packages travel when they are unmoored from the contexts of culture and politics from which they emerged and reattached as allegories within the culture and politics of those with the institutional strength to spread the word. The Chico Mendes story was transformed as an allegorical package by and for northern audiences. Mendes himself was aware of the tension between his own activist goals and northern retellings. Yet the alliance was important to him, and he negotiated skillfully between disparate positions.40 After his death, northern uses of his story were no longer under his control. And yet it was in shedding the localizing southern attachment of Mendes’s negotiations that his story became most fit to travel as a northern allegory.

原页 234

当行动主义包裹脱离其产生的文化与政治语境，并作为寓言重新附着于那些拥有传播话语的制度力量者的文化与政治中时，它们就会旅行。奇科·门德斯的故事由北方受众改造为服务于北方受众的寓言包裹。门德斯本人意识到自己的行动主义目标与北方重述之间的张力。然而联盟对他很重要，他在不同立场之间巧妙谈判。40他死后，北方对他故事的利用不再受他控制。然而，正是在摆脱门德斯谈判中地方化的南方依附时，他的故事才最适合作为北方寓言旅行。

原页 234, 235

The Burning Season, a popular HBO movie (1995) that dramatizes Mendes’s life, and in which Mendes is played by Silvia Braga, shows some possible translations for this packaging process. The movie is made for U.S. audiences; everyone speaks in English. The rubber tappers’ stand-offs against tree-cutting ranchers look suspiciously like television images of U.S. civil rights marches, with marchers linking arms and singing hymns. Masculine heroism is buoyed up by feminine communalism. The film builds its dramatic climax through juxtaposing scenes of dangerous carousing ranchers, riding and shooting and handling prostitutes, with scenes of Mendes sitting quietly among women lighting candles in church, or giving Christmas presents to his wife and children. The masculine traditions of Brazilian union politics are hardly in evidence. Here we see a key element of the northern allegory: Environmental struggles tame destructive frontier masculinity with the courage of men who represent a softer feminine or androgynous community. This allegory was written into U.S. environmental politics at the turn of the last century for John Muir (see chapter 3), and it has remained with us. Male heroics and ecofeminist communalisms strengthen each other in this story, which appeals to North Americans even as it pulls away from Brazilian roots. The Chico/Chipko pun is foreshadowed in the making of a movement of which women and gentle men might be proud. LPMA activists took their reading of Chico Mendes’s story from this very movie.41

校注8
原页 234, 235

《燃烧季节》（The Burning Season），一部颇受欢迎的 HBO 电影（1995），戏剧化了门德斯的生平，门德斯由西尔维娅·布拉加饰演，展示了这一包装过程的一些可能翻译。这部电影为美国观众制作；每个人都说英语。橡胶采集者对抗砍树牧场主的场景，看起来可疑地像美国民权游行的电视画面，游行者挽着手臂，唱着赞美诗。男性英雄气概被女性共同体主义托起。影片通过并置场景来构建戏剧高潮：危险的纵酒牧场主骑马、开枪、玩弄妓女，而门德斯安静地坐在教堂里点蜡烛的女人中间，或送给妻儿圣诞礼物。巴西工会政治的男性传统几乎不见踪影。这里我们看到北方寓言的一个关键要素：环境斗争用代表更柔和女性或中性共同体的男人的勇气，驯服破坏性的边疆男性气概。这个寓言在上个世纪之交被写入约翰·缪尔的美国环境政治（见第三章），并一直伴随着我们。男性英雄气概与生态女性主义共同体主义在这个故事中相互加强，它吸引北美观众，同时脱离巴西根源。奇科/契普科的双关在一场女人和温和男人可能为之自豪的运动的形成中被预示。LPMA 活动家正是从这部电影中获得他们对奇科·门德斯故事的解读。41

校注8
原页 235

If the Mendes package traveled in the north particularly because of this gender story, this is even more true of the Chipko tree-hugging movement, known internationally for the presence of women as well as men supportive of women’s concerns. The Chipko movement began in the 1970s in the Garwhal region of the Himalayas when the Forestry Department refused local plans for forest product development and assigned the trees to an outside company. The people demonstrated, gathering at felling sites to protect the trees. If ever a social movement has undergone multiple cultural translations, it is Chipko. The charismatic packages proliferate as both activists and scholarly portrayers vie to show the movement as a women’s movement, a Ghandian initiative, a peasant insurrection, or a pro-development protest.42 The story of the movement has become unmoored from its original context to form traveling packages. Political ecologist Haripriya Rangan (2000) argues that this unmooring has occurred through alliances with urban elites in India, who imagine the Himalayas as a sacred place for timeless nature and indigenous knowledge. The Chipko myth caters to this image. Mythic portrayals of the movement from public intellectuals in India have gained international currency. Northern activists introduce further allegorical deviations, but, in contrast to the Mendes story, it is Indian portraits of Chipko—and not rehashed northern ones—that travel most prominently.

原页 235

如果门德斯包裹在北方传播，特别是因为这个性别故事，那么对于契普科抱树运动就更是如此；该运动在国际上闻名，既因为女性的在场，也因为支持女性关切的男性在场。契普科运动始于20世纪70年代喜马拉雅加瓦尔地区，当时林业部拒绝当地关于林产品开发的计划，把树木分配给一家外部公司。人民示威，聚集在伐木地点保护树木。如果说有哪场社会运动经历过多种文化翻译，那就是契普科。随着活动家和学术描绘者竞相把这场运动展示为妇女运动、甘地式倡议、农民起义或支持发展的抗议，富有感召力的包裹不断增殖。42这场运动的故事已脱离其原初语境，形成旅行的包裹。政治生态学家哈里普里亚·兰甘（Haripriya Rangan，2000）论证说，这种脱离是通过与印度城市精英的联盟发生的，这些精英把喜马拉雅想象为永恒自然和原住民知识的圣地。契普科神话迎合这一形象。印度公共知识分子对这场运动的神话式描绘获得了国际流通。北方活动家引入更多寓言偏差，但与门德斯故事相反，流传最显著的是印度人对契普科的描绘——而不是北方人重新改编的版本。

原页 235

One of the most passionate Chipko storytellers is Vandana Shiva, an ecofeminist who has written prolifically about the crimes of globalization and corporate development. For Shiva, Chipko is a women’s movement, a mobilization of women’s indigenous knowledge and spiritual affinity with all growing things (Shiva 1992). It is an allegory of what will be lost if we follow the demands of economists, who ignore the work of women and of nature in reproducing the earth and human well-being. Shiva’s allegory has been influential in stimulating one modest but significant stream of U.N.-funded NGO and community initiatives, referred to as “Women, Environment, and Development.”43 It is on this stream that the Chipko story came to Indonesia. Yet Indonesians would never have been interested if the story had not sparked something there.

原页 235

最充满激情的契普科讲述者之一是范达娜·席瓦，一位生态女性主义者，写了大量关于全球化和公司发展罪行的作品。对席瓦来说，契普科是一场妇女运动，是妇女原住民知识及其与一切生长之物的精神亲缘的动员（Shiva 1992）。这是一个寓言，讲述如果我们听从经济学家的要求将会失去什么，这些经济学家无视妇女和自然在地球与人类福祉的再生产中所做的工作。席瓦的寓言影响了联合国资助的非政府组织和社群倡议中一股不大但重要的潮流，即“妇女、环境与发展”。43契普科故事正是沿着这股潮流来到印尼的。然而，如果这个故事没有在印尼激起什么，印尼人绝不会感兴趣。

原页 236

Speaking of Gender

Freed from national coordination, regional, ethnic, and religious politics emerged in Indonesia with force at the turn of the century. In South Kalimantan, the question of the role of Islam in defining politics was paramount. In the last years before the end of the New Order, a commitment to Islam and to political criticism had become tightly intertwined in the region. Islam provided a vocabulary and moral framework for demanding personal integrity and social justice. Most regional activism in those last years—including environmentalism—was empowered by the cosmopolitanism of religion. After 1998, however, political models from the international Left also seemed enticing to regional youth. Students practiced the vocabulary of revolution and liberation, citing Che Guevara or the Indonesian struggle for independence. In these globally inflected discussions of new political possibilities, the issue of gender stood out because of its ability to speak not only to the proper behavior of men and women but also to the interplay of their transnational and local allegiances. The dialogue between Islamic and secular Left models of politics was conducted, quietly, through negotiating gender. Without explicit reference, gender filtered into the considerations through which environmental activists weighed political options. Traveling stories of political mobilization caught the attention of local activists in part because of their gender valences.

原页 236

谈论性别

摆脱全国协调后，地区、族群和宗教政治在世纪之交强力出现在印尼。在南加里曼丹，伊斯兰在界定政治中的作用问题至关重要。在新秩序结束前的最后几年，对伊斯兰的承诺和对政治批评的承诺在该地区紧密交织。伊斯兰为要求个人正直和社会正义提供了词汇和道德框架。最后那些年的大多数地区行动主义——包括环保主义——都被宗教的世界主义赋权。然而1998年后，来自国际左派的政治模型对地区青年也显得诱人。学生练习革命与解放的词汇，引用切·格瓦拉或印尼独立斗争。在这些受全球影响的关于新政治可能性的讨论中，性别问题凸显出来，因为它不仅能谈论男女的适当行为，还能谈论他们跨国与地方忠诚的相互作用。伊斯兰与世俗左派政治模型之间的对话，是通过协商性别悄然进行的。性别在没有明确提及的情况下渗入环保活动家权衡政治选择的考量。政治动员的旅行故事吸引当地活动家，部分因为其性别效价。

原页 236

The story of the Chipko women hugging trees—and ecofeminism more generally—sparked local attention in this context. Chipko encouraged a cosmopolitan appreciation of indigenous knowledge. It supported the notion that women could have a plurality of bases for spirituality and struggle. It offered a platform for a new kind of activism in South Kalimantan, including a happy collaboration between Muslim advocates and non-Muslim Meratus Dayaks. I don’t know how to judge whether modernist Islam or spiritual pluralism offers more for Muslim women. Instead, I point to the local debates in which these varied forms of transnational inputs become charismatic. Islamic modernists and indigenous advocates respectively grasp at traveling packages to make it possible for them to do something in Kalimantan that they might not otherwise be able to accomplish. The packages offer them tools and frameworks to be political actors.

原页 236

在这种背景下，契普科女人抱树的故事——以及更广泛的生态女性主义——激发了当地关注。契普科鼓励一种对原住民知识的世界主义欣赏。它支持这样的观念：女性可以拥有灵性与斗争的多元基础。它为南加里曼丹一种新型行动主义提供了平台，包括穆斯林倡导者与非穆斯林梅拉图斯达雅克人之间幸运的合作。我不知如何判断现代主义伊斯兰还是精神多元主义为穆斯林女性提供更多。相反，我指出这些不同形式的跨国输入变得具有感召力的当地辩论。伊斯兰现代主义者和原住民倡导者各自抓住旅行的包裹，使他们有可能在加里曼丹做成一些否则无法完成的事。这些包裹为他们提供成为政治行动者的工具和框架。

原页 236, 237

In the mid-1990s, piety was the most influential discourse of reform in South Kalimantan. The demand to clean up government was moral: public responsibility begins with one’s own conscience, and the best way to end corruption is through ethical revitalization. Political meetings in these times were often prayer meetings, and brave public discussion both in and out of the university inspired heightened personal piety on the part of activists. The consequences for women were complicated. The more they joined in politics, the more drawn in they became to discourses of religious piety that required displays of modesty. There is no reason that women cannot use such discourses to further their goals, but it was challenging to form links with secular Jakarta professionals and foreign NGOs and foundations from this position.

原页 236, 237

20世纪90年代中期，虔诚是南加里曼丹最有影响的改革话语。整肃政府的要求是道德性的：公共责任始于自己的良心，结束腐败的最佳方式是通过伦理复兴。这些时期的政治会议往往是祈祷会，大学内外勇敢的公开讨论激发了活动家更高的个人虔诚。对女性的后果是复杂的。她们越是参与政治，就越被要求表现端庄的宗教虔诚话语吸引。没有理由认为女性不能利用这类话语推进自己的目标，但从这一位置与世俗的雅加达专业人士以及外国非政府组织和基金会建立联系具有挑战性。

原页 237

The rising tide of Islamic activism in the provincial capital of South Kalimantan in the 1990s was exemplified in changes in fashion for women activists. In the 1980s women only covered their hair in a Muslim fashion if they were attending religious school or if they were trying to make a fashion statement, for example, wearing a green jilbab scarf to match a green dress. But by the mid-1990s, women activists had adopted a more pious dress style. The women I met in study groups and NGO meetings were wearing full tentlike veils. As I understood it, only such a statement of extreme piety would offer one the right to speak. While male activists did not wear special clothes, their activism too was intertwined with religious goals, including the moral protection of women.

原页 237

20世纪90年代，南加里曼丹省会伊斯兰行动主义的上升浪潮，体现在女性活动家的时尚变化中。20世纪80年代，女性只有在就读宗教学校或试图作出时尚声明时，才会以穆斯林方式遮住头发，例如戴绿色 jilbab 头巾来配绿色连衣裙。但到90年代中期，女性活动家采用了更虔诚的着装风格。我在学习小组和非政府组织会议上遇到的女性穿着帐篷般的全身面纱。据我理解，只有这种极端虔诚的声明，才能赋予说话的权利。男性活动家不穿特殊服装，但他们的行动主义也与宗教目标交织，包括对女性的道德保护。

原页 237

In 1998, the fashions and precedents of the New Order began to change very rapidly. In 1997, the bravest activist T-shirt I saw in South Kalimantan read, “I am not afraid of politics.” In 2000, I saw “Revolution or Death” shirts. The women LPMA activists I met were wearing T-shirts and jeans. In the mountains, we slept and even bathed in the river at night in a mixed group. These were urban Muslims, no different in background than the veiled women I had met three years before. Instead of a single road to piety, they told me about indigenous knowledge and alternative spiritualities. They were pluralists, drawing on a mix of local and foreign cultural legacies, rather than crafting a singular morality. New possibilities had opened.

原页 237

1998年，新秩序的时尚和惯例开始迅速改变。1997年，我在南加里曼丹见过的最勇敢的活动家 T 恤上写着：“我不怕政治。”2000年，我见到“革命或死亡”的衬衫。我遇到的 LPMA 女活动家穿着 T 恤和牛仔裤。在山里，我们男女同住，甚至晚上一起在河里洗澡。这些是城市穆斯林，背景与三年前我遇到的戴面纱女性没有不同。她们向我讲述的不是一条通往虔诚的单一路径，而是原住民知识和另类灵性。她们是多元主义者，汲取本地与外国文化遗产的混合，而不是打造单一道德。新的可能性已经打开。

原页 237

My female companions in the LPMA called attention to their own stakes as women activists by reference to the term gender. This was a new term, adopted from English, and they were excited about it. They wanted me to tell them more about gender. When I asked about this, they spoke of their ability to move and travel in public despite criticisms. They wanted to walk the forest trails despite fears and stories that this was dangerous; they wanted to carry their own packs despite anxieties about their strength. Gender referred to a political stance, a subject position in which women could operate with secular authority.

原页 237

我的 LPMA 女性同伴通过“gender”一词来指出自己作为女性活动家的利害关系。这是一个新词，从英语借来，她们对它很兴奋。她们想让我多讲讲 gender。当我问起时，她们谈到自己不顾批评在公共场合移动和旅行的能力。她们想走森林小径，尽管有恐惧和危险的故事；她们想背自己的背包，尽管担心自己的力量。Gender 指的是一种政治立场，一种女性可以以世俗权威行动的主体位置。

Gender, too, formed part of a traveling package. Packages travel when they are translated in such a way as to form a significant intervention in a local scene. They are used in local debates, within which they may introduce new objects and subjects of politics. They make it possible to act within the cultural-political scenarios they promote, and they mobilize people for particular kinds of political agency.

原页 237, 238

性别也构成旅行包裹的一部分。当包裹被翻译成对当地场景构成重要干预时，它们就会旅行。它们被用于当地辩论，在其中可能引入政治的新客体与新主体。它们使人们在它们所推广的文化—政治场景中行动成为可能，并动员人们投入特定类型的政治能动性。

原页 238

Activist packages are allegories of political subjectivity. Packages are created in a process of unmooring in which powerful carriers reformulate the stories they spread transnationally. Unmooring is easy to condemn, but it is not always a terrible thing. Traveling packages are translated to become interventions in new scenes where they gather local meanings and find their place as distinctive political interventions. Gender has proven especially plastic as the term has been variously adopted.44 Yet its packages, too, carry travel histories, and particularly the histories of collaboration that engender activism. Their deployment adds new layers, revising these histories: thus the contradictory variety of international feminism. To move beyond imperial models of gender and feminism, it is important to appreciate how activists borrow traveling feminisms for their own uses.

原页 238

行动主义包裹是政治主体性的寓言。包裹在脱离的过程中被创造，有权力的携带者在其中重新表述他们跨国传播的故事。脱离容易受到谴责，但并不总是可怕的事。旅行包裹被翻译，成为新场景中的干预，在那里收集地方意义，并找到作为独特政治干预的位置。性别一词被以各种方式采纳，已被证明尤其具有可塑性。44然而它的包裹也携带旅行历史，特别是孕育行动主义的合作历史。它们的部署增加新的层次，修订这些历史：因此国际女性主义有着矛盾多样的形态。要超越性别与女性主义的帝国模型，重要的是理解活动家如何借用旅行的女性主义为自己所用。

原页 238

Meanwhile, it is important to appreciate how those packages went traveling in the first place. Packaging of the sort I have been describing has its own heritage. Late-colonial civilizing projects are an important model, with influence not only on post-colonial development but also on the gamut of projects of democracy, good governance, and human rights that surround us today. These packages carry the inequalities of global geopolitics even as they promote rhetorics of equality. Those who adopt and adapt them do not escape the colonial heritage, even as they explore its possibilities. Thus, too, international feminism and global environmentalism stretch this heritage but also depend upon it. In each case, adherents are committed to the spread of abstract principles. In practice, the principles come to us in allegorical bundles, marked by the culture and politics of particular moments of alliance and intervention.

原页 238

与此同时，重要的是理解这些包裹最初是如何开始旅行的。我一直在描述的这种包装有其自身的遗产。晚期殖民文明化项目是一个重要模型，不仅影响后殖民发展，也影响今天围绕我们的民主、善治和人权等一系列项目。这些包裹在推广平等修辞的同时，也承载着全球地缘政治的不平等。采纳并调整它们的人并未逃脱殖民遗产，即使他们在探索其可能性。因此，国际女性主义和全球环保主义也延伸了这份遗产，但同时也依赖它。在每一种情况下，追随者都致力于抽象原则的传播。在实践中，原则以寓言捆束的形式来到我们面前，带有特定联盟与干预时刻的文化和政治标记。

The post-New Order period has been a bundle of contradictions. Political life has revived in cities and towns. Meanwhile, a new level of chaos and violence has torn up much of the countryside. U.S.-led global war has encouraged a return of military rule, while military crimes of all sorts are reported everywhere. The sad destruction of the forests by Suharto’s cronies is discussed widely; at the same time, illegal resource extraction has blossomed beyond Suharto’s dreams. Corruption is criticized even as it proliferates everywhere. International conservation groups gain clout in the environmental field as Indonesia becomes poorer and more dependent: and this just at the moment radical national environmentalists worked so hard to achieve.

原页 239, 240

夏赫里尔省长：我们乐意协助。我们承认，南加里曼丹一些投资者遇到过当地人主张土地所有权的问题。我们已建议总统发布总统令：若出现此类主张，人民必须对中央政府、省政府或县政府提起法律诉讼，而不是对涉事公司或投资者。我们仍在等待这样的政策。在这种情况下起诉商人或投资者是不恰当的。（Garuda 2002: 54–55）

新秩序后时期是一团矛盾。城市和城镇的政治生活已经复兴。与此同时，新的混乱和暴力撕裂了大部分乡村。美国领导的全球战争鼓励军事统治回归，同时各地都有各种军事犯罪的报道。苏哈托亲信对森林的可悲破坏被广泛讨论；与此同时，非法资源开采的繁荣超出苏哈托的梦想。腐败受到批评，却在各地蔓延。随着印尼变得更贫穷、更依赖他人，国际保护团体在环境领域获得影响力：而这恰恰发生在激进的全国环保主义者如此努力希望促成的时刻。

原页 240

It is in this context that enforcement has become the dominant trope in conservation for the international organizations. Enough about community empowerment, they say: Let’s get the criminals. As one foreign consultant explained, “true reform demands law, order and governance in natural-resource management” (Ivereigh 2003: 29). But how shall we create order? From the international perspective, there is only one proven formula: the recognition of the exclusive rights of national and international elites to claim valuable things. We call these rights “property.”

原页 240

在这种背景下，执法已成为国际组织保护工作的主导修辞。他们说，社群赋权谈够了：让我们抓罪犯。正如一位外国顾问所解释的，“真正的改革要求自然资源管理中的法律、秩序和治理”（Ivereigh 2003: 29）。但我们如何创造秩序？从国际视角看，只有一种被证明有效的公式：承认国内和国际精英对有价值之物的排他性权利。我们把这些权利称为“财产”。

原页 240

2003. My mother sends me The Nature Conservancy’s latest magazine because it contains an article on saving wild orangutans in Kalimantan (Ivereigh 2003). Orangutans are good-looking primates with their red shaggy hair and mobile faces. Unfortunately for their future, they live in lowland tropical rainforests, eating fruits, insects, leaves, and other plant material. They reproduce slowly (a female raises at most four offspring), and they require large tracts of solitary space. As the forest is felled and fragmented, orangutans suffer and die. Survivors are shot or captured for the illegal pet trade, particularly by loggers. The conservationists who inform the article are not at all optimistic that any will survive in the wild.

原页 240

2003年。母亲寄给我大自然保护协会的最新杂志，因为里面有一篇关于拯救加里曼丹野生红毛猩猩的文章（Ivereigh 2003）。猩猩是长得好看的灵长类，有着红色蓬乱的毛发和富有表情的脸。对它们的未来而言，不幸的是，它们生活在低地热带雨林，吃果实、昆虫、树叶和其他植物材料。它们繁殖缓慢（一只雌性最多养育四个后代），需要大片独处空间。随着森林被砍伐和破碎化，猩猩受苦并死亡。幸存者被枪杀或捕获用于非法宠物贸易，尤其是被伐木者。为文章提供信息的保护主义者对任何猩猩能在野外存活一点也不乐观。

原页 240, 241

Privileged Americans, raised with stuffed animals and fuzzy pets, like big mammals, and it makes good sense to tell the story of Kalimantan’s forests to a U.S. audience through orangutans. These American preferences can be a conservation nightmare, as when people insist on the well-being of every animal even when that animal is destroying a multispecies habitat. But the synergies between wild orangutans and rainforests are only positive ones. It is impossible to protect wild orangutans without protecting forest. Orangutans don’t even steal crops or attack people; they only want to be left alone. I am willing to risk sneers about “charismatic megafauna” to support the campaign for wild orangutans; to work for wild orangutans is to work for the forest. However, the implications for the indigenous people who have lived longest with the forest are more ambiguous. Forest-dwelling peoples ought to benefit from forest protection programs. However, it is also possible to imagine conservation programs for orangutans that further rip off and displace indigenous people—even while protecting a certain amount of their socially nurtured forest. It is up to organizations such as The Nature Conservancy to determine the course. Will conservation work for or against forest-dwelling communities? Who will be conservation’s allies?

原页 240, 241

伴着毛绒玩具和毛茸茸宠物长大的特权美国人喜欢大型哺乳动物，用猩猩向美国受众讲述加里曼丹森林的故事很合理。这些美国偏好可能成为保护噩梦，例如当人们坚持每一只动物的福祉，即使那只动物正在破坏多物种栖息地。但野生猩猩与雨林之间的协同效应只有正面的。不保护森林就不可能保护野生猩猩。猩猩甚至不偷庄稼，也不攻击人；它们只想不被打扰。我愿意冒着被人嘲笑“魅力型大型动物”的风险，支持保护野生猩猩的运动；为野生猩猩工作就是为森林工作。然而，这对与森林共处最久的原住民意味着什么，则更为含混。森林居民本应受益于森林保护项目。然而，也可以想象为猩猩设计的保护项目进一步剥削和驱逐原住民——即使它保护了一定数量由社会培育的森林。方向取决于大自然保护协会等组织。保护将有利于还是不利于森林居民社群？谁将成为保护的盟友？

校注19
原页 241

Among environmental organizations, The Nature Conservancy is best known for its deep commitments to capitalism and private property. Historically, the organization imagined its mission as buying up land to protect it from development. This strategy was expanded as the Conservancy was able to solicit the donation of private lands, which either themselves become conservation lands or allow the organization to buy more ecologically valuable patches. In the 1980s and 1990s, the organization grew exponentially, becoming the world’s richest environmental group (Ottaway and Stephens 2003a). The Conservancy became known for its corporate partnerships, which range from soliciting funds to urging environmental standards in exchange for the organization’s imprimatur. This issue of the magazine, for example, includes an article on how the Conservancy has benefited from the generosity of General Motors, including U.S.$23 million of grant money in the last ten years (Wilkonson 2003). Still, the heart of the Conservancy is the preservation of land through ownership.

原页 241

在环保组织中，大自然保护协会以其对资本主义和私有财产的深刻承诺而闻名。历史上，该组织把自己的使命想象为买下土地以保护其免受开发。随着协会能够募集私人土地捐赠——这些土地或本身成为保护地，或使组织能够购买更多具有生态价值的地块——这一策略得到扩展。20世纪80和90年代，该组织指数式增长，成为世界上最富有的环保团体（Ottaway and Stephens 2003a）。协会以企业伙伴关系闻名，范围从募集资金到敦促企业遵守环境标准，并以协会的认可作为交换。例如，这一期杂志有一篇文章讲协会如何受益于通用汽车的慷慨，包括过去十年2300万美元的资助（Wilkonson 2003）。尽管如此，协会的核心仍然是通过所有权保护土地。

原页 241

This is a strategy that depends on unquestioning confidence in private property and the political economy (e.g., law; contracts; inheritance; police protection; “interest” in several senses; transnational convertibility) that makes property worthwhile. In the United States, where this political economy is rather pervasive, it is arguably a worthwhile strategy, tapping the environmental consciousness of the landed elite and holding back the tide of destructive development. Despite their disagreements with the Conservancy’s corporate policies, many U.S. environmentalists express respect for the organization’s land acquisition programs. Outside of the United States it is difficult to be so sanguine. To promote private property and corporate rights in tropical rainforests is not just advocacy for the prevailing system of inequality; it introduces a new and terrible inequality, as it supports the expropriation of land and resources from the forest's old inhabitants. If worked through properly, land rights could protect forest communities; but of all the many international organizations promoting private property in Kalimantan, none, to my knowledge, have addressed the justice of a system in which forest residents, by definition, have no property. While “benefits” may be channeled to “local communities,” property is for elites.

原页 241

这是一项依赖于对私有财产及使财产具有价值的政治经济体系（例如法律、合同、继承、警察保护、兼有利益、利息等多重含义的“interest”、跨国可兑换性）不加质疑的信心的策略。在美国，这种政治经济相当普遍，这可以说是一项有价值的策略，利用有地精英的环境意识，抵挡破坏性发展的浪潮。尽管与大自然保护协会的企业政策存在分歧，许多美国环保主义者对该组织的土地购置项目表示尊重。在美国之外，很难如此乐观。在热带雨林推广私有财产和企业权利，不只是倡导盛行不平等制度；它引入一种新的可怕不平等，因为它支持从森林原有居民手中征用土地和资源。如果处理得当，土地权可以保护森林社群；但在加里曼丹推广私有财产的众多国际组织中，据我所知，没有一个处理过这样一个制度的正义问题：森林居民按定义没有财产。尽管“利益”可能被输送给“当地社群”，财产是给精英的。

In Kalimantan, it was the Suharto regime that claimed the forests for the state, and then divided them up for the benefit of crony capitalism. Post-New Order legalities depend on this economy of theft. Companies want their fair share of the free lands created by decree; this is freedom for the rich. Some social democrats imagine the flood of immigrants, with their legal and illegal schemes, as evening out the score. But this view ignores those who already live there. From the perspective of old forest residents, legal and illegal schemes are not so different. Funded and authorized from common sources, their products find their way into common commercial pools. Legal and illegal exploiters combine forces to wrest their profits from the forest and those who depend upon it.

In contrast, the Conservancy feels that parks and nature reserves are unhelpful in the current situation. Stanley explains: “Ironically it would be counterproductive to push for a protected area. Certification can be a good thing. I am pleased to see the article mention the independent and nonprofit Forest Stewardship Council (FSC), which offers the most responsible certification program of which I know. The FSC requires that certification address land tenure and indigenous rights as well as forest sustainability. If there is going to be corporate logging—and I’m sure there is—it ought to have some framework of responsibility. Yet one independent assessment has concluded that, because of land expropriation, “certification to FSC standards in Indonesia is currently not possible” (Colchester et al. 2003: 270). Indonesian environmentalists and indigenous leaders have called for a moratorium on certification (Lawrence et al. 2003).

The result is that we imagine an imperially mandated nature, protected for the appreciation of international elites. Indigenous communities are given a symbolic nod: a one-sentence assurance that the Conservancy will “increase the benefits of local communities from legitimate timber concessions” (Ivereigh 2003: 30) and a touristic photograph. The latter is confusingly captioned: “Meanwhile, generations of Punan people (above) have lived in and relied on the forest; their culture depends on its survival—and perhaps its on theirs” (ibid.: 29). If the Punan are necessary to the forest, why aren’t they consulted in the article? Why weren’t they invited to the certification workshop, which included only industry leaders and conservation authorities? And where are Indonesian activists, democrats, community spokespeople, and environmental scientists? Are these omissions just aesthetic tactics to draw the U.S. audience of the magazine, or do they reflect the Conservancy’s policy? One fears the latter. One fears that the Conservancy’s deep faith in capitalism and private property has overridden their ability to assess the political situation. They have chosen allies, but not those who can tell them about the social world of the forest. They will have to rely on shooting poachers—with all the terrible consequences of that decision.

The series raises the question of whether capitalist accumulation and conservation objectives can work together harmoniously—in the United States as well as beyond. Even in the United States, acquisition is not politically neutral. It is a struggle for freedom—for the rich.4

Can any cause for common justice emerge across these differences?

原页 245

To ask this question well, we must move beyond the common-sense assumption that solidarity means homogeneity. Differences invigorate social mobilizations. Differences engage political abstractions, making them applicable to local situations. At the same time, differences are organized by common assumptions about political process. It is impossible to participate in a movement without representing one’s demands through its ruling discourses; no one unacquainted with the concept of freedom, for example, can make claims through it. Political mobilizations mount a generalized frame for what will count as politics, including the politics of difference. Difference is thus both a pre-established frame for connection and an unexpected medium in which connection must find local purchase.

原页 245

要恰当地提出这个问题，我们必须超越“团结意味着同质”这一常识假设。差异使社会动员充满活力。差异让政治抽象概念参与进来，使其适用于当地情境。同时，差异由关于政治过程的共同假设组织。参与一场运动，不可能不通过其主导话语来表述自己的诉求；例如，不熟悉自由概念的人，无法通过它提出主张。政治动员为“什么算作政治”——包括差异的政治——搭起一个普遍化框架。因此，差异既是连接的预先建立的框架，也是连接必须在其中找到地方落点的意外媒介。

原页 245, 246

All this means that social mobilizations are facilitated by their appeal to diverse social groups, who find divergent means and meanings in the cause. Social mobilizations are also held up and redirected by their inclusion of varied groups, who disagree about what are supposed to be common causes and objects of concern. In this process, universalist causes are locally reconfigured, even as they are held by a wider-reaching charisma.

原页 245, 246

这一切意味着，社会动员因诉诸多样社会群体而得到推动，这些群体在事业中找到不同的手段和意义。社会动员也因纳入各种群体而受阻并改变方向，这些群体对什么是共同事业和关切对象意见不一。在这一过程中，普遍主义事业被地方性地重新配置，即使它们仍由一种影响更广的感召力维系。

原页 246

One of the best places to look for this kind of friction is in the formation of collaborative objects, which draw groups into common projects at the same time as they allow them to maintain separate agendas. This chapter considers the formation of the community-managed forest as an object of advocacy. My narrative follows how a community-managed forest emerged in one time and place through the collaborative energies of village leaders in the Meratus Mountains of South Kalimantan, nature lovers from the provincial capital of Banjarmasin, and New Order-era national activists from the Indonesian capital, Jakarta. Meratus villagers, nature lovers, and activists are, of course, the three groups I have described in some detail in the preceding three chapters. As I have shown, each group has a rather different kind of commitment to nature. In this chapter, I mix up their separate stories to show what happened when these three separate commitments came together in a short—but productive—campaign. Quite against precedent, they succeeded, at least for a while, in establishing a landscape removed from corporate destruction because it could be considered a community-managed forest.

原页 246

寻找这类摩擦的最佳地点之一，是协作对象的形成——这些对象把不同群体拉入共同项目，同时允许它们维持各自议程。本章考察作为倡导对象的社群管理森林的形成。我的叙述追随社群管理森林如何在特定时空，通过南加里曼丹梅拉图斯山脉的村庄领袖、省会班贾尔马辛的自然爱好者，以及来自首都雅加达的新秩序时代全国活动家的协作能量而出现。梅拉图斯村民、自然爱好者和活动家，当然就是我在前三章中较详细描述的三组人。如我所展示的，每一组对自然都有着相当不同的承诺。在本章中，我把他们各自的故事混合起来，展示当这三种分离的承诺在一场短暂却富有成效的运动中汇合时发生了什么。完全违背先例，他们成功地把一片地景从公司破坏中移出——至少暂时如此——因为它可以被视为社群管理的森林。

Yet this common object, the forest, did not just hold them together; it also kept them apart. For a historian of these events, one of the most striking things about the campaign is the fact that the varied, and equally satisfied, protagonists never came to any agreement about what happened. The coupling of obviously divergent perspectives and campaign success gives us pause. Activists are used to linking disagreement and failure; if participants disagree, we think the campaign must have been a mistake. In this campaign, undifferentiated unity was not a prerequisite for success.

然而，这个共同对象——森林——不只是把他们维系在一起；它也使他们彼此分离。对于这些事件的历史学家来说，运动最引人注目的一点在于，那些各执一词却同样满意的当事人，从未就发生了什么达成任何一致。明显分歧的视角与运动成功的结合令人驻足。活动家习惯于把分歧与失败联系起来；如果参与者意见不一，我们就认为运动一定出了错。在这场运动中，无差异的统一并不是成功的先决条件。

原页 246, 247

Difference within common cause: Perhaps this is more important than we ordinarily think. In this chapter I propose this kind of overlapping, linking difference as a model of the most culturally productive kinds of collaboration. This is not the most common connotation of collaboration; this is collaboration with a difference: collaboration with friction at its heart. Usually, scholars think of collaborators as like-minded colleagues who each contribute to a commonly conceived product. They are trained to be just alike before they begin to work together, so their collaboration is in itself culturally uneventful. Of course, there is another meaning of collaboration that opens the term in a different direction: Collaborators work with the enemy in wartime. These collaborators are not positioned in equality or sameness, and their collaboration does not produce a communal good. This is a place to start in opening up other meanings of working together. Parties who work together may or may not be similar and may or may not have common understandings of the problem and the product. The more different they are, the more they must reach for barely overlapping understandings of the situation. Their common cause is also a cultural encounter, and the objects on which they appear to agree are most successful when they appeal simultaneously to divergent cultural legacies. Furthermore, collaborators may or may not have any understanding of each other’s agendas. Such collaborations bring misunderstandings into the core of alliance. In the process, they make wide-ranging links possible: they are the stuff of global ties. They are also the stuff of emergent politics: they make new objects and agents possible.3

原页 246, 247

共同事业中的差异：也许这比我们通常认为的更重要。在本章中，我提出这种重叠的、连接性的差异作为最具文化创造力的协作形式的一种模型。这不是协作最常见的含义；这是有差异的协作：以摩擦为核心的协作。通常，学者把合作者想象为志同道合的同事，各自为一个共同构思的产品作出贡献。他们在开始合作之前就被训练得彼此相似，因此他们的协作本身在文化上平淡无奇。当然，协作还有另一个含义，把这个词引向不同方向：合作者在战时与敌人合作。这些合作者并不处于平等或相同的位置，他们的协作不产生共同利益。这是打开“共同工作”其他含义的一个起点。共同工作的各方可能相似，也可能不相似；可能对问题和产品有共同理解，也可能没有。他们彼此差异越大，就越需要寻求对情势仅有少许重叠的理解。他们的共同事业也是一场文化遭遇，而他们似乎一致的对象，在同时诉诸不同文化遗产时最为成功。此外，合作者可能理解彼此的议程，也可能完全不理解。这类协作把误解带入联盟的核心。在这一过程中，它们使广泛的联系成为可能：它们是全球联系的原料。它们也是新兴政治的原料：它们使新的对象和行动者成为可能。3

原页 247

Community-based conservation—which depends upon such objects as community-managed forests—has become one of the most exciting agendas in environmentalist circles: to conservationists, it is the hope for on-the-ground environmental protection; to developers and social justice advocates, it returns environmentalist energies to people. At the same time, there is much to criticize in these projects, particularly in their peculiar reifications of forests, communities, and conservation. Before we follow either advocates or critics into naturalizing the object of their debates, it seems useful to ask how this object has, in various times and places, come into being. In at least one time and place, the collaborative process joined very different perspectives on people and forests; it succeeded in part because no one stopped to realize the depth of their disagreements. Collaboration was not consensus making but rather an opening for productive confusion. Productive confusion is sometimes the most creative and successful form of the collaborative production of natural and social objects—whatever their political status.

原页 247

以社群为基础的保护——依赖于社群管理森林这类对象——已成为环保圈中最激动人心的议程之一：对保护主义者来说，它是实地环境保护的希望；对发展工作者和社会正义倡导者来说，它把环保主义能量归还给人民。同时，这些项目有许多可批评之处，尤其是它们对森林、社群和保护的奇特物化。在我们跟随倡导者或批评者把其辩论对象自然化之前，先问一问这个对象如何在不同的时间和地点形成，似乎是有益的。至少在一个时间和地点，协作过程把关于人与森林的非常不同的视角连接起来；它成功的部分原因在于没有人停下来意识到他们分歧的深度。协作不是达成共识，而是为富有成效的混淆打开空间。富有成效的混淆有时是自然与社会对象协作生产中最有创造性和最成功的形式——无论其政治地位如何。

原页 247

What Happened in Manggur

原页 247

芒古尔发生了什么

原页 247

The small village of Manggur is located in the western foothills of the Meratus Mountains. The Meratus Dayak inhabitants are shifting cultivators and forest foragers. They are a small cultural minority in both the South Kalimantan region and the nation; most Indonesians, environmentalists or otherwise, have never heard of them. Yet in 1986 Manggur people played an important role in an environmentalist drama.

原页 247

小村庄芒古尔位于梅拉图斯山脉西麓。梅拉图斯达雅克居民是游耕者和森林采集者。他们在南加里曼丹地区和国家都是一个小小的文化少数群体；大多数印尼人，无论是否环保主义者，从未听说过他们。然而1986年，芒古尔人在一出环保戏剧中扮演了重要角色。

原页 247, 248

In December 1986, a meeting of environmentalists was held in Banjarmasin. The meeting was sponsored by the Indonesian network for forests, SKEPHI, an issue-oriented network affiliated with the environmentalist umbrella group WALHI. Both SKEPHI and WALHI imagined themselves at that time as national coalitions of regional grassroots groups; this meeting—SKEPHI’s first national meeting in the provinces—was a demonstration of and an “exercise” in that conception. A provincial nature lovers’ group, Kompas Borneo, hosted the meeting, which involved activists and journalists from around the nation and abroad. Kompas Borneo further demonstrated their grassroots commitment by bringing a local environmental issue to the meeting: the conflict between the inhabitants of the village of Manggur and a timber company cutting trees on the village’s traditional lands. Kompas Borneo brought a group of Manggur men to the meeting to speak, and some seventy-five meeting participants followed these men back to stay in Manggur for several days. SKEPHI and WALHI members also met with employees of the timber company, the Fast Forest Development Company; they spoke, too, with regional officials. As a result of the publicity surrounding these activities, the regional government decided not to renew rights to work the timber concession in that area. The forests returned to Meratus Dayak management. Furthermore, the newly won acclaim of the provincial group, Kompas Borneo, allowed them to garner a Ford Foundation grant to support research in the village; meanwhile, the Jakarta groups SKEPHI and WALHI moved into their strongest periods of forest and forest people’s advocacy.

原页 247, 248

1986年12月，一场环保主义者会议在班贾尔马辛举行。会议由印尼森林网络 SKEPHI 主办，这是一个以议题为导向的网络，隶属于环保伞状组织 WALHI。当时 SKEPHI 和 WALHI 都把自己想象为地区基层团体的全国联盟；这次会议——SKEPHI 首次在外省举行的全国会议——是对这一构想的一次展示和“演练”。一个省级自然爱好者团体 Kompas Borneo 主办了会议，来自全国和外国的活动家和记者参加了会议。Kompas Borneo 通过把一个当地环境问题带到会议上，进一步展示了他们的基层承诺：芒古尔村居民与一家在村庄传统土地上砍树的木材公司之间的冲突。Kompas Borneo 带了一群芒古尔男子到会上发言，约75名与会者跟随这些人回到芒古尔，在那里逗留数日。SKEPHI 和 WALHI 成员还会见了木材公司快速森林开发公司的雇员；他们也与地区官员交谈。由于这些活动引发的宣传，地区政府决定不再续批该地区伐木特许区的经营权。森林回到梅拉图斯达雅克人的管理中。此外，省级团体 Kompas Borneo 新赢得的声誉使他们获得福特基金会资助，支持在村中的研究；与此同时，雅加达团体 SKEPHI 和 WALHI 进入了其森林与森林人民倡导的最强时期。
